structures.name: Ethmoid bone
structures.what: Light midline bone between the orbits: a horizontal [[s.cribriform-plate]], a vertical perpendicular plate topped by the [[s.crista-galli]], and two lateral labyrinths of air cells whose lateral walls are the [[s.lamina-papyracea]].
structures.why: Almost all of FESS happens inside it, and its roof and lateral walls are all that separate the dissection from brain and orbit. Its turbinates and lamellae are the landmarks you count while you work.

rel.note: the orbital plates of the frontal bone roof the labyrinth (fovea ethmoidalis)

pearls.text: The ethmoid roof you see endoscopically is mostly *frontal* bone ([[s.fovea-ethmoidalis]]); the ethmoid bone itself contributes the cribriform plate and its lateral lamella.

Its turbinates (middle, superior, supreme) and the uncinate process derive from the embryologic ethmoturbinals; with the bullar lamella, their lamellae organize the labyrinth ([[s.ethmoid-ground-lamellae]]).

structures.name: Ethmoid labyrinth (ethmoid sinus)
structures.what: The paired honeycomb of ethmoid air cells ([[m.ethmoid-cell-count]]) between the nasal cavity and the orbit, divided by the [[s.basal-lamella]] into anterior and posterior groups.
structures.why: Ethmoidectomy is the backbone of FESS: opening it systematically, lamella by lamella, exposes the orbit laterally, the skull base above and the sphenoid behind.
structures.ct: Coronal: the cell block between the MT and the orbit, below the fovea; axial: the ladder of cells from the lacrimal fossa back to the sphenoid face.

pearls.text: The labyrinth is narrow in front and wider behind, while its roof slopes down posteriorly: posterior cells are fewer and larger, but the skull base is lower and the orbital apex and optic nerve are close.

Cells pneumatize beyond the labyrinth into the frontal, sphenoid, maxillary and orbital-roof regions (IFAC cells, [[v.sphenoethmoidal-cell]], [[v.infraorbital-ethmoid-cell]], [[v.supraorbital-ethmoid-cell]]); name every cell by where it arose, not where it ended up.

structures.name: Ethmoid ground lamellae (concept)
structures.what: The ethmoid is built from roughly parallel, obliquely coronal bony lamellae left by the embryonic ethmoturbinals: 1st uncinate process, 2nd bullar lamella, 3rd basal lamella of the MT, 4th lamella of the superior turbinate, 5th of the supreme turbinate when present.
structures.why: Counting lamellae front to back is how you keep your place in a diseased ethmoid: the 3rd (basal) separates anterior from posterior ethmoid, and posterior to it drainage goes to the superior meatus.

pearls.text: Lamellae are rarely flat walls: they are indented, pneumatized and incomplete. Identify each on sagittal CT before surgery rather than expecting a clean sequence.

The spaces between lamellae (the infundibulum, suprabullar/retrobullar recesses, superior meatus) are the drainage clefts; each lamella's insertion on the skull base or lamina decides which cleft a cell drains into.

structures.name: Ethmoid bulla
structures.what: Usually the largest and most constant anterior ethmoid cell, bulging into the middle meatus behind the [[s.uncinate-process]] and the [[s.hiatus-semilunaris]].
structures.why: It is the first ethmoid cell opened after uncinectomy and a guide upward: its roof leads toward the skull base, and the AEA usually crosses the roof at or just behind its lamella.
structures.ct: Coronal: the round cell above the infundibulum and lateral to the MT; sagittal: sits below the frontal recess, its anterior face forming the recess's posterior wall when the bullar lamella reaches the skull base.
structures.endo: Right, 0°, middle meatus: the rounded bulge behind the uncinate free edge; after uncinectomy, enter it inferomedially and take its walls laterally and upward.

rel.note: its ostium usually opens on the posterior or medial face into the retrobullar recess / hiatus semilunaris superior

pearls.text: Open the bulla low and medial, then remove its walls laterally to the lamina papyracea — never punch up through its roof blindly.
If the [[s.bullar-lamella]] reaches the skull base, the bulla's anterior face is the posterior wall of the frontal recess; if not, a [[s.suprabullar-recess]] opens forward into the frontal recess.
It is not pneumatized on some sides ([[v.nonpneumatized-bulla]]); the solid ridge (torus lateralis) is then easy to mistake for the lamina papyracea or the basal lamella.

structures.name: Bullar lamella
structures.what: The anterior wall of the bulla continued upward — the second ethmoid lamella — attached laterally to the lamina papyracea and, on many sides, superiorly to the skull base, where it forms the posterior wall of the frontal recess.
structures.why: Whether it reaches the skull base decides whether a suprabullar recess exists and whether the frontal recess opens backward into it; its skull-base attachment is often right beside the AEA.
structures.ct: Sagittal: the thin wall rising from the bulla roof toward the skull base behind the frontal recess; note whether it touches the roof or stops short.
structures.endo: Right, 30°, after bulla removal: the remnant wall behind the frontal recess; take it flush to the skull base only once the AEA is identified.

rel.note: when it reaches the skull base

pearls.text: The bullar lamella at the skull base is the posterior limit of the frontal recess; clearing it last, from anterior to posterior with a 45° or 70° view, exposes the AEA without surprise.

structures.name: Suprabullar recess
structures.what: Air space between the roof of the bulla and the skull base, present when the bullar lamella does not reach the skull base.
structures.why: It communicates forward with the frontal recess and backward with the retrobullar recess, and the AEA often crosses its roof — so it is both a route into the frontal recess and a place the artery is cut.
structures.ct: Sagittal: air above the bulla roof and below the fovea, continuous anteriorly with the frontal recess.
structures.endo: Right, 30°, over the bulla after anterior ethmoidectomy: a cleft above the bulla roof leading up to the skull base.

rel.note: when the bullar lamella is deficient superiorly

pearls.text: Suprabullar cells ([[v.suprabullar-cell]], [[v.suprabullar-frontal-cell]]) arise here and push the frontal drainage pathway forward.

structures.name: Retrobullar recess
structures.what: Cleft between the posterior wall of the bulla and the basal lamella, opening medially into the middle meatus.
structures.why: It is the space you open to reach the basal lamella; the bulla usually drains into it.
structures.endo: Right, 0°, middle meatus: the cleft behind the bulla, lateral to the MT, seen after medializing the MT gently.

structures.name: Basal lamella of the middle turbinate
structures.what: The lateral attachment of the middle turbinate — the third ethmoid lamella — a bony sheet running from the skull base to the lamina papyracea that divides anterior from posterior ethmoid cells.
structures.why: Cells in front drain to the middle meatus, cells behind to the superior meatus; perforating it inferomedially is the controlled entry into the posterior ethmoid.
structures.ct: Sagittal: the S-shaped plate behind the bulla, vertical anteriorly and turning horizontal posteriorly; axial: the oblique line from the MT to the lamina.
structures.endo: Right, 0°, after bulla removal: the flat wall facing you behind the retrobullar recess, lateral to the MT.

pearls.text: The MT has three attachments: vertical to the skull base (at the lateral lamella/cribriform junction), the basal lamella to the lamina papyracea, and posteriorly to the crista ethmoidalis just in front of the sphenopalatine foramen.
Enter it at the junction of its vertical and horizontal parts, medially and inferiorly, just above the horizontal part — away from both skull base and orbit.
Preserve the horizontal part: it keeps the MT stable after full ethmoidectomy and prevents lateralization.
It is often pushed forward or back by retrobullar and posterior ethmoid cells, so its CT shape is sinuous — find it on sagittal slices first.

structures.name: Basal lamella, vertical part
structures.what: Anterior, near-coronal part of the basal lamella, running from the skull base down to the lamina papyracea behind the bulla.
structures.why: This is the wall perforated to enter the posterior ethmoid; superiorly it meets the skull base where the retrobullar recess ends.

structures.name: Basal lamella, horizontal part
structures.what: Posterior, near-axial part of the basal lamella attaching along the lamina papyracea and medial orbital floor, ending at the MT's posterior attachment near the crista ethmoidalis.
structures.why: It anchors the MT: resecting it (or the posterior MT attachment) risks a floppy, lateralizing MT and bleeding from SPA branches near the crista ethmoidalis.

structures.name: Anterior ethmoid cells
structures.what: Ethmoid cells anterior to the basal lamella — agger nasi, bulla, suprabullar and retrobullar cells and the cells of the frontal recess — all draining to the middle meatus.
structures.why: Their disease drives most chronic rhinosinusitis and they sit directly against the thinnest skull base (the lateral lamella, at their medial roof) and beside the AEA.

rel.note: and behind it; the frontal recess, at the front of the anterior ethmoid, connects the two

structures.name: Posterior ethmoid cells
structures.what: Ethmoid cells behind the basal lamella, usually fewer and larger, draining into the superior (or supreme) meatus.
structures.why: Here the skull base is lower and the orbit and optic nerve are closer; a posterior ethmoid cell may extend over the sphenoid and carry the optic nerve in its wall ([[v.sphenoethmoidal-cell]]).
structures.ct: Coronal: cells above the level of the horizontal basal lamella, behind the globe, with the skull base lower than anteriorly; axial: last cells before the sphenoid face.
structures.endo: Right, 0°, through the basal lamella: larger cells whose roof is the skull base and whose lateral wall is the posterior lamina papyracea.

rel.note: and lateral: the ostium opens medial to the superior turbinate ([[pr.sphenoid-ostium-medial-to-st]]), so a transethmoid sphenoidotomy is made low and medial

pearls.text: The skull base is best identified here — cells are large and the roof is broad — then followed forward ([[pr.skull-base-posterior-to-anterior]]).
The medial rectus lies against the posterior lamina with little intervening fat: no powered instrument toward the lamina here.

structures.name: Superior meatus
structures.what: Narrow channel under and lateral to the superior turbinate, into which the posterior ethmoid cells drain.
structures.why: Its posterior end leads to the sphenoethmoidal recess; resecting the lower part of the superior turbinate here exposes the sphenoid ostium medial to it.
structures.endo: Right, 0°/30°, passed medial to the MT into the olfactory cleft: the slit under the superior turbinate.

rel.note: mucociliary flow runs back through the sphenoethmoidal recess to the nasopharynx

structures.name: Fovea ethmoidalis (ethmoid roof)
structures.what: The roof of the ethmoid labyrinth: the medial orbital plate of the frontal bone, dimpled by the cells below it, joining the lateral lamella medially.
structures.why: It is the skull base you touch during ethmoidectomy; relatively thick laterally, it joins the far thinner lateral lamella medially — injuries cluster at that junction.
structures.ct: Coronal bone window: the roof line over the ethmoid; its medial end steps down via the lateral lamella to the cribriform plate — that step is the Keros depth ([[c.keros]]).
structures.endo: Right, 0°/30°, after complete ethmoidectomy: smooth, whitish bone thicker than the cell septa, sloping downward from anterior to posterior; the AEA crosses it anteriorly and the PEA posteriorly.

pearls.text: The skull base slopes downward from anterior to posterior; aim instruments along that slope, not horizontally, in the posterior ethmoid.
Skull-base bone usually looks thicker and more ivory-white than the ethmoid septations — a useful cue that becomes unreliable in osteitic or revision cavities.
Roof height can differ between sides ([[v.asymmetric-ethmoid-roof]]); read each side separately on coronal CT.
Skull-base cells (suprabullar, supraorbital) dimple the roof; the smooth roof between dimples is where you can safely run a curette forward.

structures.name: Lateral lamella of the cribriform plate
syn: lateral lamella of the cribriform plate
structures.what: Thin vertical bony wall rising from the lateral edge of the cribriform plate to the fovea ethmoidalis — the medial wall of the ethmoid roof and the lateral wall of the olfactory fossa.
structures.why: The thinnest bone of the anterior skull base and the commonest site of iatrogenic CSF leak; the deeper the olfactory fossa, the more of it faces your instruments.
structures.ct: Coronal bone window: the vertical or oblique segment joining cribriform plate to fovea; measure its height ([[c.keros]]), its angle ([[c.gera]]) and compare sides.
structures.endo: Rarely seen directly; right, 0°/30°: the medial ethmoid roof just lateral to the MT's skull-base attachment — the MT's vertical lamella hangs from its lower end.

pearls.text: Dissect toward the lamina (lateral), not along the MT attachment (medial): the ethmoid roof is weakest medially.
The MT's vertical lamella attaches here; twisting or pulling the MT can fracture it — cut the MT sharply, never avulse it.
The AEA pierces it at the [[s.anterior-ethmoidal-sulcus]], where it is thinnest — a site of both iatrogenic and spontaneous CSF leak.

structures.name: Cribriform plate
structures.what: Horizontal perforated plate on each side of the crista galli forming the floor of the olfactory fossa; the olfactory fila pass through its foramina from the nasal mucosa to the olfactory bulb.
structures.why: It roofs the olfactory cleft and is the lowest, most medial part of the anterior skull base; entry here means CSF leak and smell loss.
structures.ct: Coronal: the lowest horizontal segment of the skull base beside the crista galli, below the fovea; its foramina make it look discontinuous — do not mistake that for a defect ([[m.cribriform-length]]).
structures.endo: Right, 0°, into the olfactory cleft between septum and MT: the roof of the cleft; not dissected in routine FESS.

pearls.text: The MT vertical lamella attaches at the cribriform/lateral lamella junction: the MT is the medial boundary of safe ethmoid dissection.
A transcribriform resection removes it between the laminae papyraceae, from the frontal sinus posterior table to the planum sphenoidale; the AEA and PEA are divided at the orbit to devascularize it.

structures.name: Olfactory fossa
syn: olfactory recess of the skull base
structures.what: Intracranial trough bounded by the cribriform plate below, the lateral lamella laterally and the crista galli medially, holding the olfactory bulb.
structures.why: Its depth is the Keros depth: the deeper it is, the lower the cribriform plate lies below the ethmoid roof and the taller the exposed lateral lamella.

pearls.text: The anterior attachment of the MT is the endoscopic guide to it: the olfactory fossa lies above and medial to the MT's vertical attachment. In many patients the most anterior part of the MT inserts on the frontal sinus floor in front of the cribriform plate, which is why that segment can be taken in a Draf IIb/III as long as the dissection stays anterior to the first olfactory fibre ([[lm.first-olfactory-fiber]]).

structures.name: Olfactory cleft
structures.what: Narrow slit high in the nasal cavity between the septum and the middle/superior turbinates, directly under the cribriform plate, lined by olfactory mucosa.
structures.why: Obstruction (polyps, edema, scarring) causes smell loss and stripping its mucosa causes permanent loss; a unilateral mass here is a skull-base lesion until proven otherwise.
structures.ct: Coronal: the air slit between septum and MT under the cribriform plate; unilateral opacification or bony erosion needs MRI.
structures.endo: Right, 0°, scope passed between septum and MT head: a narrow slit with tan-yellow mucosa superiorly.

pearls.text: Never biopsy a unilateral olfactory-cleft mass before CT and MRI: esthesioneuroblastoma, encephalocele and meningioma all present here.

structures.name: Olfactory mucosa
structures.what: Specialized sensory neuroepithelium lining the roof of the olfactory cleft, the upper septum and the medial surfaces of the superior and upper middle turbinates.
structures.why: Every incision or resection near the cleft trades against smell: keep septal flap incisions and turbinate resections below it and do not strip cleft mucosa.

structures.name: Olfactory fila (olfactory nerve)
structures.what: Bundles of unmyelinated olfactory axons (CN I) passing from the olfactory mucosa through the cribriform plate to the bulb, each sleeved by dura and arachnoid.
structures.why: Avulsing them (MT twisting, cleft stripping) causes anosmia and can open a CSF path along their sleeves; the most anterior fibre is the posterior limit of a Draf III ([[lm.first-olfactory-fiber]]).
structures.endo: Right, 0°/30°, in the anterior olfactory cleft after removing the anterior-superior septum (Draf III): a small fibre and pit running up into the cribriform plate just behind the frontal sinus floor.

rel.note: first olfactory fibre = posterior limit of the drill-out

structures.name: Olfactory bulb
structures.what: Oval swelling at the front of the olfactory tract lying on the cribriform plate in the olfactory fossa, receiving the fila.
structures.why: Olfactory-groove meningiomas and esthesioneuroblastomas involve it; transcribriform resection sacrifices it on the involved side (sometimes one side can be preserved).

structures.name: Olfactory tract
structures.what: Band running back from the olfactory bulb in the olfactory sulcus of the frontal lobe, lateral to the gyrus rectus, to the olfactory trigone.
structures.why: Marks the lateral edge of the gyrus rectus in transcribriform and transbasal exposures; preserved on the uninvolved side when oncologically safe.

structures.name: Crista galli
structures.what: Midline triangular crest of the ethmoid projecting up into the anterior cranial fossa between the olfactory bulbs; the falx cerebri attaches to it.
structures.why: The midline anchor of the anterior skull base: it is drilled down and the falx divided in transcribriform approaches, and a pneumatized crista can hide a mucocele or mimic a cell.
structures.ct: Coronal: the midline bony spike above the cribriform plates; may be pneumatized ([[v.crista-galli-pneumatization]]).
structures.endo: Exposed from below only in a transcribriform approach: right/left, 0°, midline above the resected upper septum.

rel.note: continuous below with the perpendicular plate

structures.name: Foramen caecum
structures.what: Small midline pit between the frontal crest and the crista galli; in the fetus a dural diverticulum passes through it toward the nasal dorsum.
structures.why: Incomplete regression explains nasal dermoids, gliomas and frontoethmoidal encephaloceles: a midline nasal mass with a widened foramen caecum or bifid crista galli needs MRI before any biopsy or excision.

rel.note: inconstant emissary vein from the nose to the sinus in children

structures.name: Anterior ethmoidal artery
structures.what: Branch of the ophthalmic artery that leaves the orbit through the anterior ethmoidal foramen, crosses the ethmoid roof obliquely (posterolateral to anteromedial), enters the olfactory fossa through the lateral lamella and then descends into the nose beside the crista galli.
structures.why: It is the key landmark of the anterior skull base and the posterior limit of frontal recess dissection — and, if cut and allowed to retract into the orbit, the classic cause of orbital hematoma.
structures.ct: Coronal: the beak-like notch in the medial orbital wall where the canal leaves the orbit, typically on the slice where the superior oblique and medial rectus are both seen; sagittal: at the skull base behind the bullar lamella, usually in the suprabullar recess (in cadaver dissection it ran between the bullar and basal lamellae on every side); check whether it runs in the roof or below it.
structures.endo: Right, 30°/45°, after anterior ethmoidectomy: a bony ridge or free-hanging vessel crossing the roof obliquely, anteromedially, at the posterior margin of the frontal recess.

rel.note: in the orbit, between superior oblique above and medial rectus below

pearls.text: Treat the AEA as the posterior margin of the frontal recess: work in front of it for frontal surgery, and never cauterize it with monopolar current near the orbit.

It hangs in a mesentery below the skull base on a substantial minority of sides ([[v.aea-in-mesentery]]) — more often with a [[v.supraorbital-ethmoid-cell]] and a deep olfactory fossa — and that is when it gets cut.

Rule of thumb along the orbital wall: about 24 mm from the anterior lacrimal crest to the AEA, about 12 mm to the PEA, about 6 mm to the optic canal ([[m.alc-to-aea]], [[m.aea-to-pea]], [[m.pea-to-optic-canal]]).

Of the two ethmoidal arteries it is the larger and the one that matters in epistaxis: it supplies the anterior third of the septum and lateral wall, while the PEA feeds only a small area around the superior turbinate and the adjacent septum. Bleeding that persists high and anterior after [[p.spa-ligation]] points to it ([[p.aea-ligation]]).

After crossing the lateral lamella it gives the [[s.anterior-falcine-artery]] and turns down through the cribroethmoidal foramen into the nose; dividing it at the orbit or skull base devascularizes olfactory-groove meningiomas.

structures.name: Anterior ethmoidal foramen
structures.what: Opening in the medial orbital wall, at or just within the frontoethmoidal suture, through which the AEA and anterior ethmoidal nerve leave the orbit.
structures.why: The target of external AEA ligation and the point from which the anterior ethmoidal canal crosses the roof; it marks skull-base level from the orbital side.

pearls.text: Externally, elevate periorbita behind the posterior lacrimal crest and follow the frontoethmoidal suture back: the first vessel tenting the periorbita is the AEA.
Double or accessory foramina occur; a foramen between AEF and PEF usually carries a [[s.middle-ethmoidal-artery]].

structures.name: Posterior ethmoidal foramen
structures.what: Opening in the frontoethmoidal suture behind the AEF, transmitting the posterior ethmoidal artery and (inconstant) nerve.
structures.why: The last landmark before the optic canal in external or endoscopic dissection along the medial orbital wall.

structures.name: Anterior ethmoidal canal
structures.what: Bony canal carrying the AEA and nerve across the ethmoid roof from the orbit to the lateral lamella; it may lie in the roof, hang below it on a bony-mucosal mesentery, or be partly dehiscent.
structures.why: Its position relative to the roof decides how exposed the artery is: a canal hanging below the roof is easily cut when clearing the frontal recess or suprabullar cells.
structures.ct: Coronal: a small round or tubular density crossing from the orbital notch toward the lateral lamella; if seen separated from the roof by air, the artery is in a mesentery.

pearls.text: Bony dehiscence of the canal wall occurs on a minority of sides ([[v.anterior-ethmoidal-canal-dehiscence]]); treat a thin ridge crossing the roof as a naked artery.

structures.name: Anterior ethmoidal sulcus
structures.what: The notch where the anterior ethmoidal canal meets the lateral lamella and the AEA passes into the olfactory fossa.
structures.why: The thinnest spot of the anterior skull base: a preferred site for both iatrogenic injury and spontaneous CSF leak, and the place where an AEA stump can retract intracranially.

structures.name: Posterior ethmoidal artery
structures.what: Smaller branch of the ophthalmic artery crossing the posterior ethmoid roof, usually just in front of the sphenoid face and optic canal; small or absent on some sides.
structures.why: It marks the posterior ethmoid–sphenoid junction and warns that the optic canal is only millimetres behind.
structures.ct: Coronal: a small notch at the frontoethmoidal suture in the posterior medial orbital wall, near the slices where the orbital apex cone forms.
structures.endo: Right, 0°/30°, posterior ethmoid roof: a fine transverse ridge, usually flush with the roof, a few millimetres in front of the sphenoid face.

rel.note: with the adjacent posterosuperior septum — a small territory next to the AEA's

pearls.text: Seeing the PEA means the optic canal is close ([[m.pea-to-optic-canal]]) — switch to gentle, visualized instruments.

Cutting it by accident is usually a minor bleed, but it can be large when an anterior skull-base tumor has recruited it or after sphenopalatine ligation has shifted flow to the ethmoidal system — seal it before dividing in those patients.
It supplies the planum dura and posterior olfactory mucosa; in transcribriform and transplanum resections it is coagulated at the lamina to devascularize the tumor base.

structures.name: Middle ethmoidal artery
structures.what: Inconstant third ethmoidal branch of the ophthalmic artery crossing the ethmoid roof between the AEA and PEA through its own small foramen.
structures.why: An unexpected vessel on the roof between AEA and PEA; do not mistake it for the AEA when counting distances from the lacrimal crest.

structures.name: Anterior ethmoidal nerve
structures.what: Branch of the nasociliary nerve (V1) accompanying the AEA through the foramen, canal and olfactory fossa into the nose, ending as the external nasal nerve on the dorsum.
structures.why: It travels in the same canal or mesentery as the AEA; its injury gives numbness of the anterior septum and nasal tip.

structures.name: Anterior falcine artery
structures.what: Branch of the AEA arising in the olfactory fossa and running up along the anterior falx.
structures.why: A feeder of olfactory-groove and falcine meningiomas and a source of bleeding when the falx is divided in transcribriform surgery.

structures.name: Frontal bone
structures.what: The forehead bone: a vertical squama containing the frontal sinuses and horizontal orbital plates that form the orbital roofs and the ethmoid roof (fovea ethmoidalis).
structures.why: Most of the skull base you meet in FESS belongs to it; its sinus is the hardest one to reach and keep open.

structures.name: Frontal sinus
structures.what: Paired, usually asymmetric air spaces in the frontal bone between the anterior and posterior tables, separated by an intersinus septum; each drains through an ostium in its floor into the frontal recess.
structures.why: Its posterior table borders brain and its floor the orbit; its narrow outflow is where most frontal sinus surgery succeeds or fails.
structures.ct: Sagittal: the hourglass of sinus, ostium and recess with the nasal beak in front; axial: the tables and intersinus septum; coronal: the floor over the orbit and the recess below.
structures.endo: Right, 70°, from below after frontal recess clearance: the dome of the sinus with the posterior table facing you and the intersinus septum medially.

rel.note: medial part of the orbital roof

pearls.text: It develops late — absent on imaging in young children and enlarging through adolescence — so small or absent frontal sinuses are common in children and in some adults ([[v.frontal-sinus-aplasia]]).
Count the cells, then decide the extent: the grade of surgery ([[c.efss]], [[c.draf]]) should match the pathology and anatomy, not habit.

It pneumatizes up into the vertical (squamous) frontal bone and back into the horizontal orbital plate, between the frontal lobe above and the orbit below; that supraorbital extension is the part an endoscope reaches worst.

The anteroposterior depth at the ostium decides whether a Draf IIb or III is feasible; measure it on the sagittal CT for each side. Authors measure it differently — nasal beak to posterior table at the ostium, or from the forward projection of the olfactory fossa to the anterior table — but the question is the same: will a drill fit in front of the skull base? About 10 mm is often quoted as the minimum, and a posterior table less than 5 mm from the skin in front of the nasal beak rules out a Draf III.

structures.name: Frontal sinus anterior table
syn: anterior wall of the frontal sinus
structures.what: The thick anterior wall of the frontal sinus under the forehead and brow.
structures.why: Trephination and the osteoplastic flap go through it; an outer-table fracture is mainly a cosmetic problem, while the outflow tract and posterior table decide management of a frontal fracture.

pearls.text: Thick diploic bone — about 4–12 mm in a textbook range — under skin, subcutaneous fat, frontalis and pericranium. In acute infection it is the wrong way in (osteomyelitis, intracranial spread): trephines enter through the floor.

structures.name: Frontal sinus posterior table
syn: posterior wall of the frontal sinus
structures.what: The thinner posterior wall separating the frontal sinus from the anterior cranial fossa dura and frontal lobes.
structures.why: Drills, trephines and fractures breach it into the cranial cavity; mucoceles erode it. In Draf III it is identified first and never drilled.

pearls.text: Inferiorly the posterior table becomes the skull base: follow it down to the first olfactory fibre and never drill behind that line ([[lm.frontal-t]]).

structures.name: Frontal sinus floor
structures.what: Floor of the frontal sinus: medially the ostium and nasal beak region, laterally the roof of the orbit.
structures.why: Draf IIa, IIb and III are progressively wider removals of this floor; an external trephine can enter the sinus through its medial part.

structures.name: Frontal intersinus septum
structures.what: Bony septum between the right and left frontal sinuses; often deviated, sometimes multiple, and sometimes pneumatized ([[v.frontal-septal-cell]]).
structures.why: It is removed in Draf III to make a common cavity; its deviation changes which sinus lies over which orbit and where a trephine lands.

structures.name: Frontal (nasal) beak
syn: nasal spine of the frontal bone
structures.what: The thick bony prominence where the frontal bone meets the nasal bones and frontal processes of the maxilla, forming the anterior-inferior margin of the frontal ostium.
structures.why: It narrows the ostium from in front; drilling it forward (Draf IIb, III) is how the ostium is enlarged anteroposteriorly.
structures.ct: Sagittal: the dense bone projecting back under the frontal sinus in front of the ostium.
structures.endo: Right, 30°/45°, looking up from the middle meatus: the thick anterior lip of the ostium; after Draf III it is drilled until the anterior curve of the new opening is smooth.

structures.name: Frontal sinus ostium
structures.what: The narrowest part of the hourglass between the frontal sinus above and the frontal recess below — the opening in the sinus floor just behind the nasal beak.
structures.why: Frontal surgery is graded by what you do to it: leave it (Draf I), clear cells through it, or enlarge it (Draf IIa, IIb, III).
structures.ct: Sagittal: the waist of the hourglass behind the nasal beak and in front of the skull base.
structures.endo: Right, 70°, after clearing the frontal recess: the funnel opening leading up into the dark sinus; confirm with a curved probe passing up without resistance.

structures.name: Frontal recess
structures.what: The inverted-funnel space below the frontal ostium through which the frontal sinus drains to the middle meatus or the ethmoid infundibulum; its walls are made by the cells around it.
structures.why: It is the most complex part of FESS: its shape is set by the agger nasi and other IFAC cells, and scarring here causes iatrogenic frontal sinusitis and mucocele.
structures.ct: Build it on all three planes: identify each cell in coronal, axial and sagittal, then trace the drainage pathway from the ostium down around them ([[pr.frontal-building-blocks]]).
structures.endo: Right, 30°/45°/70°, from the middle meatus above the MT axilla: a cleft behind or medial to the agger nasi cell, in front of the bulla; a curved probe passed up it enters the sinus.

rel.note: usual; the pathway can be medial, posteromedial or rarely lateral to it
the MT vertical lamella forms its medial wall
medial to the uncinate when it inserts on the lamina (terminal recess present); into the ethmoid infundibulum when the uncinate inserts on the skull base or MT ([[c.uncinate-superior-attachment]])

pearls.text: Boundaries: anterior — agger nasi cell and nasal beak; posterior — bullar lamella/bulla and the AEA; medial — MT vertical lamella; lateral — lamina papyracea; above — the frontal ostium.
Remove cell caps by fracturing them up and away from the pathway ('uncapping the egg') and never strip mucosa circumferentially.

Anterior cells (agger nasi, supra agger, supra agger frontal) push the pathway medially, posteriorly or posteromedially; posterior cells (suprabullar, suprabullar frontal, supraorbital ethmoid) push it anteriorly; a frontal septal cell pushes it laterally, often posteriorly ([[c.ifac]]).

structures.name: Terminal recess
structures.what: The blind upper end of the ethmoid infundibulum formed when the uncinate process inserts laterally on the lamina papyracea (or agger nasi cell).
structures.why: Its presence means the frontal sinus drains medial to the uncinate directly into the middle meatus; the recess itself is a dead end — do not mistake it for the frontal ostium.

rel.note: separated from it by the uncinate's superior attachment

structures.name: Agger nasi
structures.what: The mound on the lateral nasal wall just in front of and above the MT's anterior attachment; when pneumatized it contains the agger nasi cell.
structures.why: The external landmark for the agger nasi cell and the frontal recess behind it; the axillary flap is raised here.
structures.endo: Right, 0°, looking at the lateral wall: the gentle bulge anterosuperior to the MT head and axilla.

structures.name: Agger nasi cell
structures.what: The most anterior ethmoid cell: a cell either anterior to the origin of the MT or sitting directly above its most anterior insertion into the lateral nasal wall.
structures.why: It is the key to the frontal recess: the pathway usually runs medial and posterior to it, so removing its roof and posterior wall exposes the recess.
structures.ct: Coronal: the first cell anterior to or above the MT's anterior attachment, at the level of the lacrimal fossa; sagittal: the anterior cell under the nasal beak with the pathway behind it; axial: anterolateral cell beside the lacrimal sac.
structures.endo: Right, 30°/45°, above the MT axilla: the bulge anterior to the frontal recess, entered through an axillary flap or through its posterior or medial wall from the recess.

rel.note: anterior to or directly above its anterior insertion
below the frontal sinus floor; its roof is uncapped to reach the frontal recess behind or medial to it

pearls.text: Present on nearly every side on CT (98.5% in Bolger's series); if you cannot find it, look again before naming a cell above it.
The uncinate often inserts on its posteromedial wall; its roof is the floor of any supra agger or supra agger frontal cell above it.
Trace on sagittal and axial CT whether the pathway passes behind it (usual), medial to it, or rarely lateral to it — that decides which wall you remove first.

structures.name: Orbit
structures.what: Bony cone holding the globe, extraocular muscles, fat, vessels and nerves; its medial wall (the lamina papyracea) is the lateral wall of the ethmoid.
structures.why: Every ethmoid dissection happens millimetres from it; orbital injury is the most common family of major FESS complications.

pearls.text: Check the eye during every ethmoidectomy: keep the eyes uncovered in the field and feel/press the globe while watching the lamina ([[pr.orbital-ballottement]]).

structures.name: Lamina papyracea
structures.what: Paper-thin lateral wall of the ethmoid labyrinth and the main part of the medial orbital wall.
structures.why: The lateral limit of every ethmoidectomy: a breach exposes orbital fat, and behind it lie the periorbita and medial rectus.
structures.ct: Coronal: the thin line between ethmoid cells and orbit; look for dehiscence, fat herniation and medial bowing ([[v.lamina-papyracea-dehiscence]]).
structures.endo: Right, 0°, after bulla removal: a smooth, flat lateral wall, often slightly translucent; the orbit lies directly behind it.

pearls.text: Find it early (after uncinectomy and a wide antrostomy) and keep it in view; it is the plane you dissect along from front to back.
Its upper border, the frontoethmoidal suture, carries the ethmoidal foramina: from the orbit side it marks the height of the skull base.
In thyroid eye disease raised orbital pressure often bows it medially into the ethmoid, so it lies closer than usual during the ethmoidectomy of a decompression.
Its curve continues smoothly into the orbital floor: following that contour up from the floor predicts where the lamina runs when osteitic partitions hide it in revision surgery.

structures.name: Frontoethmoidal suture
structures.what: Suture on the medial orbital wall between the orbital plate of the frontal bone above and the lamina papyracea below; the ethmoidal foramina lie along it.
structures.why: It marks ethmoid-roof level from the orbital side: stay below it in external ethmoidectomy and decompression, and follow it to find the ethmoidal arteries.

structures.name: Periorbita
structures.what: The periosteum lining the bony orbit, loosely attached except at sutures, fissures and the rim; continuous with dura at the optic canal and superior orbital fissure.
structures.why: It holds orbital fat back: a bony breach with intact periorbita rarely matters, a torn periorbita means fat in the field and the medial rectus at risk. In decompression it is incised deliberately.
structures.endo: Right, 0°, after removing the lamina: a glistening grey-white sheet that bulges when the globe is pressed.

structures.name: Orbital fat
structures.what: Extraconal and intraconal fat filling the orbit around the muscles, globe and optic nerve.
structures.why: Fat in the field means the periorbita is open: stop any powered instrument there. In decompression, controlled fat prolapse is the goal.
structures.endo: Yellow lobules that move when the globe is pressed; unlike ethmoid polyps they do not bleed and they float in saline.

pearls.text: Medially, the extraconal fat lies between the periorbita and the medial rectus, crossed above the muscle by the ethmoidal neurovascular bundles; inside the muscle cone the intraconal fat surrounds the optic nerve and vessels, and the inferior intraconal space carries the oculomotor branches to the inferior rectus and inferior oblique. Extraconal fat may be coagulated and removed; intraconal fat is left alone.

structures.name: Medial rectus
structures.what: Extraocular muscle along the medial orbital wall, separated from the lamina papyracea only by periorbita and a thin fat layer that thins further posteriorly.
structures.why: Injury, usually by a powered instrument through a lamina breach, causes severe permanent diplopia.
structures.ct: Coronal: the soft-tissue band just lateral to the lamina at mid-orbit, beside the ethmoid cells; note the fat plane between muscle and lamina.

pearls.text: Posteriorly the muscle lies almost on the lamina: a small breach in the posterior ethmoid is closer to muscle than the same breach anteriorly.

The medial intraconal space beside it is divided by the inferomedial muscular trunk of the ophthalmic artery into zone A (anteroinferior — most accessible; the oculomotor branch enters the muscle's inner surface posteriorly), zone B (anterosuperior, beside the ethmoidal vessels, sometimes reached above the muscle) and zone C (behind the arterial trunk — smallest and hardest, next to the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery).

structures.name: Superior oblique
structures.what: Extraocular muscle running forward along the superomedial orbit to the trochlea, where its tendon turns back to the globe.
structures.why: It lies just above the level of the ethmoidal foramina; on coronal CT the AEA notch sits between it and the medial rectus, and external medial approaches can injure it or its trochlea.

structures.name: Trochlea
structures.what: Fibrocartilaginous pulley in the trochlear fossa of the frontal bone at the superomedial orbital rim, through which the superior oblique tendon turns.
structures.why: Elevation off the trochlear fossa (Lynch incision, frontal trephination, osteoplastic flap margins) must stay subperiosteal so the trochlea resuspends — otherwise diplopia.

structures.name: Medial canthal tendon
structures.what: Tendon anchoring the medial eyelid canthus to the anterior and posterior lacrimal crests, enclosing the lacrimal sac between its limbs.
structures.why: External approaches (Lynch, external ethmoidectomy, external AEA ligation) must avoid it or repair it precisely; detachment causes telecanthus.

structures.name: Orbital roof
syn: orbital plate of the frontal bone
structures.what: Orbital plate of the frontal bone; medially it floors the frontal sinus and continues medially as the fovea ethmoidalis over the ethmoid.
structures.why: A supraorbital ethmoid cell pneumatizes into it behind the frontal sinus; mistaking that cell for the frontal sinus leaves the true sinus obstructed.

structures.name: Orbital floor
structures.what: Floor of the orbit and roof of the maxillary sinus, crossed by the infraorbital canal.
structures.why: Casiano's key landmark: its medial part seen through a wide antrostomy fixes the height at which to enter the posterior ethmoid and sphenoid; in inferomedial decompression it is removed medial to the infraorbital nerve.
structures.endo: Right, 30°/45°, through a wide maxillary antrostomy: the smooth roof of the antrum with the infraorbital canal ridge running forward.

structures.name: Inferomedial orbital strut
structures.what: Thickened bony buttress at the junction of the orbital floor and medial orbital wall.
structures.why: Preserving it in endoscopic decompression limits inferomedial globe displacement and reduces new postoperative diplopia, at the cost of somewhat less decompression.

structures.name: Inferior rectus
structures.what: Extraocular muscle running along the orbital floor.
structures.why: Enlarged in thyroid eye disease and at risk (with the infraorbital nerve) when the floor is removed in decompression.

structures.name: Orbital apex
structures.what: The narrow posterior end of the orbit, where the optic canal and superior orbital fissure open, bounded medially by the posterior ethmoid and sphenoid.
structures.why: Posterior ethmoid dissection and apex decompression meet here; vision is at risk from mechanical, thermal or compressive injury.

structures.name: Common tendinous ring
structures.what: A fibrous ring at the orbital apex from which the four rectus muscles arise. It encircles the orbital opening of the [[s.optic-canal]] and the middle part of the [[s.superior-orbital-fissure]], and blends with the [[s.periorbita]] and the dural sheath of the optic nerve.
structures.why: It is the tightest collar around the optic nerve as the nerve enters the orbit, so an [[p.optic-nerve-decompression]] is carried forward to it. The medial and superior recti arise closest to the nerve: a sheath incision extended through the ring can detach their origins and cause diplopia ([[h.medial-rectus-injury]]), and the ophthalmic artery runs below and lateral to the nerve inside it.
structures.endo: Either side, 0°/30°, after the lamina papyracea and medial optic canal wall are removed: a thicker, whiter band where the periorbita meets the optic nerve sheath at the orbital end of the canal.

rel.note: to the bone around the canal's orbital opening
spans its middle part (the oculomotor foramen)
both divisions, through the fissure part of the ring

pearls.text: Inside the ring run the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery (through the canal) and CN III, the nasociliary nerve and CN VI (through the fissure); the lacrimal, frontal and trochlear nerves and the superior ophthalmic vein pass above it, outside the muscle cone.

structures.name: Supraorbital nerve
structures.what: Terminal branch of the frontal nerve (V1) leaving the orbit through the supraorbital notch or foramen to supply the forehead and scalp.
structures.why: Brow and coronal incisions for trephination or osteoplastic flap must spare it or accept forehead and scalp numbness.

structures.name: Supratrochlear nerve
structures.what: Branch of the frontal nerve (V1) exiting the orbit just above the trochlea to supply the medial forehead.
structures.why: The nerve most at risk from a medial brow incision for trephination.

structures.name: Anterior cranial fossa
structures.what: The floor of the cranial cavity under the frontal lobes: orbital plates of the frontal bone laterally, cribriform plate and crista galli medially, planum sphenoidale and lesser wings posteriorly.
structures.why: Its floor is the roof of the ethmoid and the olfactory cleft; its dura, olfactory apparatus and frontal lobes are what an anterior skull-base breach exposes.

structures.name: Anterior cranial fossa dura
structures.what: Dura lining the anterior cranial fossa; tightly adherent over the cribriform plate, where it sleeves the olfactory fila, and thin over the lateral lamella.
structures.why: Breach means CSF leak; its adherence at the cribriform explains why small bony injuries there leak. It is resected and reconstructed in transcribriform surgery.

structures.name: Gyrus rectus
structures.what: The most medial gyrus on the orbital surface of the frontal lobe, above the cribriform plate and medial to the olfactory sulcus and tract.
structures.why: The first brain seen above the olfactory groove in transcribriform approaches; it is gently retracted or, rarely, resected to reach olfactory-groove lesions.

structures.name: Falx cerebri
structures.what: Sickle-shaped dural fold in the interhemispheric fissure, anchored anteriorly to the crista galli.
structures.why: Divided at its anterior base in bilateral transcribriform resections to join the two sides; the anterior falcine artery runs in it.

structures.name: Superior sagittal sinus (anterior part)
structures.what: Midline dural venous sinus along the attached upper border of the falx, beginning anteriorly near the foramen caecum.
structures.why: Its anterior part is at risk in bifrontal and transcribriform exposures, and frontal sinusitis can spread to it through valveless diploic veins (thrombosis, intracranial abscess).

structures.name: Frontopolar artery
structures.what: Branch of the A2 segment of the anterior cerebral artery running forward along the medial frontal lobe toward the frontal pole.
structures.why: Found on the superior-posterior capsule of large olfactory-groove meningiomas: dissect it free, do not coagulate it.

structures.name: Medial orbitofrontal artery
structures.what: First cortical branch of the anterior cerebral artery, usually from proximal A2, running forward over the gyrus rectus and orbital surface of the frontal lobe.
structures.why: It lies directly on top of olfactory-groove and planum lesions exposed endonasally; injury risks frontal infarction.

structures.name: Sinonasal bony envelope (reconstruction)
structures.what: The bone within 12 mm of the named air spaces in the reference specimen, drawn as one surface for orientation; it is a reconstruction unit, not an anatomical structure.
structures.why: Gives the specimen its skeleton while the walls pack carries the named bones.

landmarks.name: Anterior lacrimal crest
landmarks.locate: Palpable ridge on the frontal process of the maxilla forming the anterior margin of the lacrimal fossa; the zero point of the 24-12-6 rule.

landmarks.name: Anterior ethmoidal foramen
landmarks.locate: Orbital opening of the anterior ethmoidal canal at the frontoethmoidal suture, medial orbital wall.

landmarks.name: Posterior ethmoidal foramen
landmarks.locate: Orbital opening of the posterior ethmoidal canal at the frontoethmoidal suture, in front of the optic canal.

landmarks.name: AEA crossing the ethmoid roof
landmarks.locate: Midpoint of the anterior ethmoidal canal on the ethmoid roof, seen endoscopically at the posterior margin of the frontal recess.

landmarks.name: AEA entry through the lateral lamella
landmarks.locate: Where the anterior ethmoidal canal meets the lateral lamella medially and the artery enters the olfactory fossa.

landmarks.name: PEA crossing the ethmoid roof
landmarks.locate: The posterior ethmoidal canal on the posterior ethmoid roof, a few millimetres anterior to the sphenoid face.

landmarks.name: Frontal ostium (centre)
landmarks.locate: Centre of the narrowest cross-section of the frontal sinus outflow on sagittal CT, behind the nasal beak.

landmarks.name: Nasal beak (posterior tip)
landmarks.locate: Most posterior point of the nasal beak projecting under the frontal ostium, on the midsagittal plane of each sinus.

landmarks.name: Posterior wall at the frontal ostium
landmarks.locate: Point on the posterior table/skull base directly behind the nasal beak at the level of the ostium; the AP distance to the beak is the working depth for Draf IIb/III.

landmarks.name: Fovea–lateral lamella junction
landmarks.locate: Coronal CT: the angle where the fovea ethmoidalis turns down into the lateral lamella; upper end of the Keros measurement.

landmarks.name: Cribriform plate, lateral edge
landmarks.locate: Coronal CT: the lateral edge of the cribriform plate where the lateral lamella begins; lower end of the Keros measurement.

landmarks.name: Cribriform plate, anterior end
landmarks.locate: Most anterior olfactory foramen, just behind the frontal sinus posterior table/foramen caecum.

landmarks.name: Cribriform plate, posterior end
landmarks.locate: Posterior margin of the cribriform plate at its junction with the planum sphenoidale.

landmarks.name: Basal lamella entry point
landmarks.locate: Inferomedial part of the basal lamella at the junction of its vertical and horizontal parts, lateral to the MT: the safe entry into the posterior ethmoid.

landmarks.name: Bullar lamella at the skull base
landmarks.locate: Where the bullar lamella meets the ethmoid roof (when it does): posterior limit of the frontal recess, commonly beside the AEA.

landmarks.name: Crista galli apex
landmarks.locate: Top of the crista galli in the midline of the anterior cranial fossa.

landmarks.name: First olfactory fibre
landmarks.locate: The most anterior olfactory filum entering the cribriform plate, just posterior to the frontal sinus floor on each side of the septum; posterior limit of a Draf III. A small emissary vein just in front of it, running laterally, is easily mistaken for it and must not be taken as the limit.

landmarks.name: Frontal T
landmarks.locate: Endoscopic (0°/30°) Draf III view: the T formed by the posterior edge of the resected superior septum (stem) and the posterior frontal sinus floor/first olfactory fibres on both sides (crossbar); drilling stays in front of it.

landmarks.name: Medial orbital floor
landmarks.locate: Junction of the orbital floor (maxillary sinus roof) and the lamina papyracea, seen through a wide middle meatal antrostomy; Casiano's height reference.

landmarks.name: Orbital apex
landmarks.locate: Point where the medial orbital wall meets the optic canal and superior orbital fissure.

landmarks.name: Inferomedial strut
landmarks.locate: Mid-point of the bony junction between orbital floor and medial wall, behind the nasolacrimal canal.

landmarks.name: Supraorbital notch
landmarks.locate: Notch or foramen on the superior orbital rim at roughly the junction of its medial and middle thirds; palpable through the brow.

landmarks.name: Frontal trephination point
landmarks.locate: Medial floor of the frontal sinus under the medial brow, medial to the supraorbital notch and lateral to the midline, chosen on CT where the sinus is deepest; not so far inferomedial that the scar reaches the frontal recess.

variants.name: Supra agger cell
deprecated: Kuhn type 2 frontal cell (tier of cells)
variants.def: IFAC: an anterolateral ethmoid cell located above the agger nasi cell that does not pneumatize into the frontal sinus. CT: sits on the agger nasi roof, below the level of the frontal ostium on sagittal/coronal views; may be single or stacked.
variants.why: It narrows the recess from in front: the pathway usually runs medial or posteromedial to it. Remove it after the agger nasi cap, fracturing its roof forward and laterally.

prev.population: adult maxillofacial CTs without sinus disease, 100 patients (200 sides), three readers
prev.note: Single IFAC CT series; other IFAC series in other populations report different rates, and pre-IFAC Kuhn type 1–2 rates are not comparable.

variants.name: Supra agger frontal cell
variants.def: IFAC: an anterolateral ethmoid cell that extends above the agger nasi into the frontal sinus. A small one reaches only the sinus floor; a large one may extend far into the sinus, even to its roof. CT: the cell crosses the level of the frontal ostium on sagittal and coronal views.
variants.why: It lies inside the frontal sinus anteriorly and laterally, and the pathway runs medial and posterior to it; incompletely removed, its roof left in the sinus is a classic cause of persistent frontal disease. A large one often needs a 70° view, curved instruments or a Draf IIa, occasionally an above-and-below approach.

prev.population: adult maxillofacial CTs without sinus disease, 100 patients (200 sides), three readers
prev.note: Single IFAC CT series; rates depend on the population and on the reader's threshold for 'extends into the sinus'.

variants.name: Suprabullar cell
variants.def: IFAC: a cell above the ethmoid bulla that does not enter the frontal sinus. CT: sagittal view shows a cell between the bulla roof and the skull base, below the level of the frontal ostium.
variants.why: It forms the posterior wall of the lower frontal recess and pushes the pathway anteriorly; the AEA often runs in or at its roof. In frontal balloon dilation ([[p.balloon-sinus-dilation]]) a well-pneumatized suprabullar cell is the classic false target: a wire in it lights the forehead as a diffuse glow, not the sharp spot that moves with a wire in the frontal sinus.

prev.population: adult maxillofacial CTs without sinus disease, 100 patients (200 sides), three readers
prev.note: Single IFAC CT series; other series spread widely because some readers count any cell above the bulla, others only distinct cells with their own roof on the skull base.

variants.name: Suprabullar frontal cell
variants.def: IFAC: a cell that originates in the suprabullar region and pneumatizes along the skull base into the posterior region of the frontal sinus; the skull base forms its posterior wall.
variants.why: It pushes the pathway anteriorly, and its posterior wall is the skull base: open it from in front, never by pushing up along the skull base behind it; the AEA often lies at its posteroinferior margin.

prev.population: adult maxillofacial CTs without sinus disease, 100 patients (200 sides), three readers
prev.note: Single IFAC CT series; other series report higher rates — the boundary with a suprabullar cell (does it reach the sinus?) is reader-dependent.

variants.name: Supraorbital ethmoid cell
variants.def: IFAC: an anterior ethmoid cell that pneumatizes around, anterior to or posterior to the AEA over the roof of the orbit. It often forms part of the posterior wall of an extensively pneumatized frontal sinus, separated from it only by a bony septum. CT: axial slices show a second air space lateral and posterior to the frontal sinus over the orbit; coronal slices show it over the orbital roof lateral to the recess.
variants.why: Its opening lies posterolateral to the frontal drainage pathway, so the true frontal ostium is anterior and medial to it — a surgeon who opens only the SOEC leaves the frontal sinus blocked. It is associated with an AEA hanging below the skull base (in cadaver dissection, 1–8 mm below the roof when the cell was large).

prev.population: adult maxillofacial CTs without sinus disease, 100 patients (200 sides), three readers
prev.note: Single IFAC CT series. Older cadaver and CT series used broader definitions (any supraorbital pneumatization) and are not comparable.

variants.name: Frontal septal cell
variants.def: IFAC: a medially based cell of the anterior ethmoid or inferior frontal sinus, attached to or located within the intersinus septum, associated with the medial side of the frontal outflow.
variants.why: It pushes the pathway laterally and often posteriorly; it may drain into either frontal sinus and is removed in a Draf IIb or III.

prev.population: adult maxillofacial CTs without sinus disease, 100 patients (200 sides), three readers
prev.note: Single IFAC CT series; other series differ widely, partly because a pneumatized intersinus septum is read differently.

variants.name: Sphenoethmoidal (Onodi) cell
variants.def: A posterior ethmoid cell that pneumatizes lateral and/or superior to the sphenoid sinus, so the optic nerve (sometimes the ICA) runs in its lateral or superior wall. CT: on coronal slices, a horizontal septum is seen within the 'sphenoid' — the cell above it is the Onodi cell; on axial slices, a posterior ethmoid cell extends behind the anterior sphenoid face lateral to the sphenoid.
variants.why: The surgeon who thinks they are already in the sphenoid is in the Onodi cell with the optic nerve in its wall: identify it on CT, open the true sphenoid medially and inferiorly, and never remove the lateral wall of the last posterior ethmoid cell blindly.

prev.note: CT series; lower values with strict criteria (optic nerve in the wall) than with 'any cell over the sphenoid'.
Cadaver dissection finds far more than CT, mostly because of definition and detection; population also matters (East Asian series report higher rates).

variants.name: AEA in a mesentery below the skull base
variants.def: The anterior ethmoidal canal hangs below the ethmoid roof, attached to it by a thin bony or mucosal lamella, instead of running within the roof. CT: coronal slices show the canal as a dot or tube separated from the fovea by air.
variants.why: This is the artery that gets cut while clearing the frontal recess or suprabullar cells; if transected it can retract into the orbit and cause an orbital hematoma. Predictors: a supraorbital ethmoid cell and a deep olfactory fossa.

prev.note: Cadaveric, not a CT prevalence: the artery hung below the roof in all 10 sides with a large supraorbital ethmoid cell and in 1 of 18 without one; 6 sides with a small cell had it close to or within the roof. CT series spread widely (slice thickness, threshold for 'below the roof') and need their own source before a CT range is quoted. A textbook chapter from the same school (Naidoo & Wormald) quotes 36% of cases in a mesentery and 16% both mesenteric and dehiscent — the most exposed combination — without denominator or method; it probably draws on the group's cadaver work but was not checked against it, so the primary cadaver figure stands.

variants.name: Anterior ethmoidal canal dehiscence
variants.def: Partial absence of the bony wall of the anterior ethmoidal canal, usually its inferior wall, so the artery is covered only by mucosa.
variants.why: A dehiscent canal looks like a thin mucosal ridge; curettes and debriders catch the naked artery.

prev.population: 70 sagittally divided adult Korean cadaver heads
prev.note: Moon attributed the ~40% reported by earlier studies to counting the small foramina of the anterior ethmoidal nerve and veins as dehiscence; the definition drives the spread. Denominator (hemi-heads) as reported, not re-checked against the full text.

variants.name: Lamina papyracea dehiscence
variants.def: Congenital or post-traumatic gap in the lamina with orbital fat or medial rectus herniating toward the ethmoid. CT: coronal slices show discontinuity of the medial orbital wall with fat density medial to the expected wall line.
variants.why: Fat or muscle can be mistaken for polyp and taken with a debrider; identify it on CT, report it, and never run a powered instrument against that wall.

prev.note: Includes both congenital dehiscence and old fractures; higher rates when minor gaps are counted.

variants.name: Frontal sinus aplasia or hypoplasia
variants.def: Absence (aplasia) or minimal pneumatization (hypoplasia) of one or both frontal sinuses. CT: no air cell above the orbital rim level in the frontal bone.
variants.why: An absent sinus changes the operation: symptoms are not frontal sinusitis, trephination and osteoplastic flaps are unsafe without image guidance, and Draf III may be impossible.

prev.note: Unilateral aplasia/hypoplasia; spread reflects whether hypoplasia is counted.

variants.name: Asymmetric ethmoid roof
variants.def: The right and left ethmoid roofs lie at different heights on coronal CT (with corresponding differences in olfactory fossa depth).
variants.why: Skull-base injuries occur more often on the lower side; read each side separately and do not assume the roof you found on one side predicts the other.

variants.name: Deep olfactory fossa (Keros type III)
variants.def: Olfactory fossa depth (lateral lamella height) 8–16 mm on coronal CT.
variants.why: A tall, exposed lateral lamella sits far below the fovea: the medial ethmoid roof is at high risk of perforation and CSF leak, and the AEA is more likely to hang in a mesentery.

prev.note: Later CT series vary widely by population (Keros II is usually the most common); per-side vs per-patient reporting also differs.

variants.name: Near-horizontal lateral lamella (Gera class III)
variants.def: Lateral lamella making an angle of less than 45° with the horizontal plane of the cribriform plate on coronal CT.
variants.why: A flat lateral lamella extends laterally under the ethmoid cells, so a lateral-looking roof may be lamella: the highest-risk configuration for skull-base injury in Gera's scheme.

variants.name: Pneumatized crista galli
variants.def: Air within the crista galli, communicating with the frontal sinus or anterior ethmoid. CT: air density inside the midline crest above the cribriform plates.
variants.why: Can be mistaken for an ethmoid cell and opened into the anterior cranial fossa, or become obstructed and form a mucocele; it is uncommon.

variants.name: Middle ethmoidal artery present
variants.def: A third ethmoidal artery and foramen between the AEA and PEA.
variants.why: It breaks the 24-12-6 count: the second vessel met along the frontoethmoidal suture may not be the PEA.

prev.note: Small cadaver series with different definitions of a separate foramen.

variants.name: Non-pneumatized bulla (torus lateralis)
variants.def: The bulla is a solid bony ridge rather than an air cell.
variants.why: A solid bulla can be misread as the lamina papyracea or basal lamella; confirm on CT before taking it.

variants.name: Bullar lamella not reaching the skull base
variants.def: The bullar lamella stops short of the ethmoid roof, leaving a suprabullar recess continuous with the frontal recess. CT: sagittal slices show air above the bulla roof communicating forward with the frontal recess.
variants.why: The frontal recess then opens posteriorly into the suprabullar recess, and the AEA lies exposed in that recess roof; the posterior limit of the frontal recess becomes the AEA/skull base rather than the bulla face.

classifications.name: International Frontal Sinus Anatomy Classification (IFAC)
classifications.basis: Each frontal recess cell is named by its position relative to the frontal sinus drainage pathway (anterior, posterior or medial) and by whether it pneumatizes into the frontal sinus, read on triplanar CT. The class tells you which way the cell pushes the pathway.

classes.label: Agger nasi cell (anterior)
classes.criterion: Cell either anterior to the origin of the MT or sitting directly above its most anterior insertion into the lateral nasal wall.
classes.why: Pathway usually medial, posterior or posteromedial to it; rarely lateral.

classes.label: Supra agger cell (anterior)
classes.criterion: Anterolateral ethmoid cell above the agger nasi cell, not pneumatizing into the frontal sinus.
classes.why: Pathway usually medial or posteromedial to it.

classes.label: Supra agger frontal cell (anterior)
classes.criterion: Anterolateral ethmoid cell extending into the frontal sinus; small ones reach only the floor, large ones may reach the roof.
classes.why: Pathway medial and posterior to it; its dome inside the sinus is what is left behind in failed surgery.

classes.label: Suprabullar cell (posterior)
classes.criterion: Cell above the ethmoid bulla that does not enter the frontal sinus.
classes.why: Pushes the pathway anteriorly; AEA often at its roof.

classes.label: Suprabullar frontal cell (posterior)
classes.criterion: Cell originating in the suprabullar region that pneumatizes along the skull base into the posterior frontal sinus; the skull base forms its posterior wall.
classes.why: Pathway anterior to it; dissect it from the front, never along the skull base behind it.

classes.label: Supraorbital ethmoid cell (posterior)
classes.criterion: Anterior ethmoid cell pneumatizing around, anterior to or posterior to the AEA over the orbital roof, often forming part of the posterior wall of the frontal sinus.
classes.why: Its opening is posterolateral; the true frontal pathway is anterior and medial to it. Predicts an AEA below the skull base.

classes.label: Frontal septal cell (medial)
classes.criterion: Medially based cell of the anterior ethmoid or inferior frontal sinus attached to or within the intersinus septum.
classes.why: Pushes the pathway laterally and often posteriorly.

classifications.caveats: Classify each side separately and name every cell present — cells combine. The pathway's relation to the uncinate process is a separate axis ([[c.uncinate-superior-attachment]]): with a lamina papyracea insertion the frontal sinus drains medial to the uncinate; with a skull-base or MT insertion it drains into the ethmoid infundibulum. IFAC replaces the Kuhn/Bent frontal cell types 1–4, frontal bullar cell and interfrontal sinus septal cell, whose prevalences are not directly comparable.

classifications.name: Extent of Endoscopic Frontal Sinus Surgery (EFSS)
classifications.basis: Grades what was done to the frontal recess cells and the frontal ostium, from dilation without tissue removal to bilateral floor removal.

classes.label: Balloon dilation
classes.criterion: Balloon dilation of the frontal drainage pathway without tissue removal.
classes.why: Done with [[p.balloon-sinus-dilation]]: nothing is removed, so the outflow is widened by displacing the cells around it rather than clearing them.

classes.label: Recess clearance, ostium untouched
classes.criterion: Clearance of frontal recess cells not directly obstructing the frontal ostium.

classes.label: Clearance of cells obstructing the ostium
classes.criterion: Clearance of cells directly obstructing the frontal ostium, without entering the sinus.

classes.label: Clearance of cells into the sinus
classes.criterion: Clearance of cells pneumatizing through the ostium into the frontal sinus, without enlarging the ostium.

classes.label: Ostium enlarged
classes.criterion: Clearance of cells pneumatizing into the sinus with enlargement of the frontal ostium (Draf IIa equivalent).

classes.label: Unilateral floor removal to the septum
classes.criterion: Enlargement of the frontal ostium from the lamina papyracea to the nasal septum (Draf IIb equivalent).

classes.label: Bilateral floor removal
classes.criterion: Removal of the frontal sinus floors bilaterally with the upper septum and intersinus septum (Draf III / EMLP equivalent).

classifications.caveats: Grade wording here is paraphrased from Wormald et al. 2016; check the source table. Unlike Draf I, EFSS separates clearing cells from enlarging the ostium.

classifications.name: Draf classification of endonasal frontal sinus drainage
classifications.basis: Extent of frontal sinus floor removal.

classes.label: Simple drainage
classes.criterion: Anterior ethmoidectomy including clearance of frontal recess cells, leaving the frontal ostium itself untouched.
classes.why: Enough for most chronic rhinosinusitis when the ostium is normal.

classes.label: Extended drainage, lateral
classes.criterion: Removal of the frontal sinus floor between the lamina papyracea and the middle turbinate.
classes.why: For cells through the ostium, mucoceles, and disease needing a wider single-side opening.

classes.label: Extended drainage, to the septum
classes.criterion: Removal of the frontal sinus floor between the lamina papyracea and the nasal septum, taking the anterior-superior MT attachment.
classes.why: Wider unilateral opening; drilling is usually needed at the nasal beak.

classes.label: Median drainage (EMLP)
classes.criterion: Bilateral type IIb plus resection of the upper nasal septum and the intersinus septum, creating one common frontal opening.
classes.why: Salvage for recalcitrant frontal disease, frontal tumors, large mucoceles, and access to the frontal sinus for skull base surgery.

classifications.caveats: Draf I in the original description includes clearing cells from the frontal recess; EFSS grades 1–3 subdivide that work. Terms modified endoscopic Lothrop procedure (EMLP) and frontal drill-out are synonyms for type III. Type I is defined inconsistently: some atlases limit it to removing the upper uncinate while leaving the agger nasi cell, whereas Draf's description and the IFAC/EFSS literature include clearing the obstructing recess cells below the ostium — state the definition when comparing results.

classifications.name: Keros classification of olfactory fossa depth
classifications.basis: Height of the lateral lamella, i.e. depth of the olfactory fossa below the level of the fovea ethmoidalis, measured on coronal images.

classes.label: Shallow
classes.criterion: Olfactory fossa depth 1–3 mm.

classes.label: Intermediate
classes.criterion: Olfactory fossa depth 4–7 mm.

classes.label: Deep
classes.criterion: Olfactory fossa depth 8–16 mm.
classes.why: Tall exposed lateral lamella far below the fovea; highest risk of medial roof perforation.

classifications.caveats: Keros described skulls; on CT the measurement depends on slice and plane. Sides often differ — classify each. Depth alone misses the angle of the lamella ([[c.gera]]).

classifications.name: Gera classification of the lateral lamella
classifications.basis: Angle between the lateral lamella and the horizontal plane through the cribriform plate on coronal CT.

classes.label: Steep
classes.criterion: Angle greater than 80°.

classes.label: Intermediate
classes.criterion: Angle 45–80°.

classes.label: Flat
classes.criterion: Angle less than 45°.
classes.why: Lamella extends laterally under the ethmoid; highest risk.

classifications.caveats: Thresholds as published by Gera et al. 2018 (class I >80° low, II 45–80° medium, III <45° high risk); the risk grades are anatomical reasoning, not measured injury rates. Use with Keros depth: a deep and flat lamella is the worst combination.

classifications.name: Chandler classification of orbital complications of sinusitis
classifications.basis: Anatomic stage of orbital involvement from sinusitis, mainly ethmoid.

classes.label: Preseptal cellulitis (inflammatory edema)
classes.criterion: Eyelid edema anterior to the orbital septum; vision and motility normal.

classes.label: Orbital cellulitis
classes.criterion: Diffuse orbital tissue inflammation without abscess; chemosis, proptosis, may limit motility.

classes.label: Subperiosteal abscess
classes.criterion: Pus between the lamina papyracea and periorbita, displacing the globe; seen on contrast CT.
classes.why: Drain if vision is threatened, it enlarges or fails medical therapy ([[p.subperiosteal-abscess-drainage]]).

classes.label: Orbital abscess
classes.criterion: Pus within the orbital tissues.

classes.label: Cavernous sinus thrombosis
classes.criterion: Spread through valveless ophthalmic veins; bilateral signs, cranial neuropathies, sepsis.

classifications.caveats: Stages are not a strict sequence — stage V can occur without IV. Contrast CT separates II, III and IV; clinical visual assessment drives urgency.

measurements.name: Anterior lacrimal crest to AEA foramen
measurements.what: Distance along the medial orbital wall from the anterior lacrimal crest to the anterior ethmoidal foramen (the '24' of 24-12-6).
measurements.note: Reported means cluster around 22–25 mm with individual variation of several millimetres; use as orientation in external approaches, never as a stop sign.

measurements.name: AEA to PEA foramen
measurements.what: Distance between the anterior and posterior ethmoidal foramina along the frontoethmoidal suture (the '12').
measurements.note: Individual values vary by several millimetres; a middle ethmoidal artery can sit between them.

measurements.name: PEA foramen to optic canal
measurements.what: Distance from the posterior ethmoidal foramen to the orbital opening of the optic canal (the '6').
measurements.note: Can be only a few millimetres: the PEA is a warning that the optic nerve is immediately behind.

measurements.name: Anterior lacrimal crest to optic canal
measurements.what: Total distance from the anterior lacrimal crest to the optic canal along the medial orbital wall.
measurements.note: Sum of the 24-12-6 rule; shorter orbits (children, some adults) shrink every segment.

measurements.name: Olfactory fossa depth (Keros)
measurements.what: Vertical height of the lateral lamella from the cribriform plate to the fovea ethmoidalis.
measurements.note: Keros distribution: type I 12%, II 70%, III 18% of skulls. CT series differ by population; measure each side.

measurements.name: Depth of the AEA below the skull base
measurements.what: Vertical distance between the anterior ethmoidal canal and the ethmoid roof when the artery runs in a mesentery.
measurements.note: Cadaveric, not CT: without a supraorbital cell the artery lay at the roof in all but one side. On CT the value also depends on slice thickness and on whether distance is taken to the canal centre or its upper edge.
measurements.population: latex-injected cadaver sides with a large supraorbital ethmoid cell (10 of 34)

measurements.name: Number of ethmoid cells per side
measurements.what: Count of anterior plus posterior ethmoid air cells in one labyrinth.
measurements.note: Textbook ranges vary; counts depend on how incomplete septa are treated.

measurements.name: Cribriform plate length
measurements.what: Anteroposterior length of the cribriform plate from its first to its last olfactory foramen.
measurements.note: Approximate; the plate is only a few millimetres wide on each side.

measurements.name: Draf III neo-ostium narrowing
measurements.what: Loss of neo-ostium area after endoscopic modified Lothrop procedure.
measurements.note: Most narrowing happens in the first year, then stabilizes; make the opening as large as the anatomy allows and cover bone with mucosa or free grafts.

measurements.name: Draf III long-term patency
measurements.what: Proportion of endoscopic modified Lothrop neo-ostia patent or only partially stenosed at last endoscopic follow-up.
measurements.note: Pooled from 18 studies (612 patients), counting partial stenosis as patent. Failure needing further surgery was 13.9% (85/612) and symptoms improved in about 82%, so patency overstates success; definitions of failure (symptoms vs closure vs revision) differ between series.

measurements.name: Endoscopic CSF leak repair success
measurements.what: Success of transnasal endoscopic CSF leak repair at the first attempt.
measurements.note: About 97% after a second repair; success depends on site (lateral sphenoid and frontal leaks are harder) and on raised intracranial pressure.

measurements.name: Proptosis reduction after endoscopic orbital decompression
measurements.what: Reduction in exophthalmometry after endoscopic medial (with or without inferomedial) wall decompression.
measurements.note: Larger with added lateral wall or fat decompression; smaller when the inferomedial strut is preserved. A textbook chapter reports an average globe recession of about 3.5 mm (range 2–12 mm) after endoscopic decompression and roughly 2 mm more with an added lateral wall decompression (expert-reported, series not specified).

measurements.name: Major complication rate of FESS
measurements.what: Rate of major complications (orbital, intracranial, major hemorrhage) in a large FESS series.
measurements.note: Combined multi-surgeon historical series; CSF leak was the most common major complication, and minor complications (mostly orbital penetration and MT adhesions) occurred in 6.9%; modern registry data vary with definitions and with revision and extended cases.

hazards.name: Lateral lamella perforation (CSF leak)
hazards.site: Medial ethmoid roof at the MT's skull-base attachment, especially at the AEA's entry (anterior ethmoidal sulcus); deep (Keros III), flat (Gera III) or asymmetric roofs.
hazards.mechanism: An instrument pushed upward or medially along the MT attachment, a twisted MT, or a curette pulled across the lamella fractures the thinnest bone of the skull base and tears the adherent dura.
hazards.consequence: CSF rhinorrhea, meningitis risk, pneumocephalus; if deeper, frontal lobe or vessel injury.
hazards.prevent: Read Keros depth, Gera angle and asymmetry on CT (CLOSE); dissect lateral, not medial, at the roof; cut the MT sharply rather than avulsing it; follow the roof from posterior to anterior.
hazards.recognize: Intraoperative: clear fluid washing blood away (washout sign) at the medial roof, a pulsating defect or dura seen. Postoperative: unilateral clear watery rhinorrhea increasing with leaning forward; confirm with beta-2 transferrin or beta-trace protein and localize with thin-section CT.
hazards.rescue: Repair at once if recognized: define the bony margins, remove mucosa from a rim around the defect, and seal with a free mucosal or fascia graft (underlay if feasible) plus overlay, supported by absorbable packing. Missed leaks: endoscopic repair, lumbar drain only selectively.

hazards.name: AEA transection
hazards.site: Posterior margin of the frontal recess, suprabullar recess roof, especially when the artery hangs in a mesentery or a supraorbital ethmoid cell is present.
hazards.mechanism: A debrider, curette or through-biter catches a canal that hangs below the roof or is dehiscent; the lateral stump retracts into the orbit and keeps bleeding behind the periorbita.
hazards.consequence: Brisk nasal bleeding; orbital hematoma with rising orbital pressure and risk of vision loss; rarely intracranial bleeding if the medial stump retracts through the lamella.
hazards.prevent: Locate the canal on coronal and sagittal CT; identify the artery at the posterior frontal recess before clearing cells there; no powered instruments on a ridge crossing the roof; keep frontal dissection anterior to it.
