Open cells between their septations rather than cutting across them — the artery can run inside one. In extended frontal or skull-base work a mesenteric artery can be bipolared deliberately early instead of risking a tear later.
hazards.recognize: Pulsatile bleeding at the roof behind the frontal recess; then eyelid swelling, proptosis, tense globe, subconjunctival hemorrhage, pupil change.
hazards.rescue: Bipolar the visible stump — never monopolar, whose current can crack the thin roof (CSF leak) and spread into the orbit; if the stump has retracted and the orbit tightens, manage as orbital hematoma ([[h.orbital-hematoma]]) — canthotomy/cantholysis and medial orbital decompression, with external ligation if bleeding continues.

hazards.name: Orbital hematoma (orbital compartment syndrome)
hazards.site: Retrobulbar or extraconal space behind a breached lamina or a retracted AEA/PEA.
hazards.mechanism: Arterial bleeding (retracted ethmoidal artery) raises pressure within minutes; venous bleeding from orbital fat after a lamina breach develops over hours. Pressure in the closed orbit compresses the optic nerve and its blood supply.
hazards.consequence: Ischemic optic neuropathy and permanent vision loss; in rhesus monkeys, complete central retinal artery occlusion for 97 minutes caused no detectable retinal damage, with progressive damage beyond about 100 minutes — an animal threshold for total occlusion, not a safe human window; arterial hematomas need decompression within minutes.
hazards.prevent: Protect the lamina and ethmoidal arteries (CLOSE review, [[pr.orbital-ballottement]]); keep the eyes in the field; stop anticoagulants appropriately; avoid tight nasal packing after a lamina breach.
hazards.recognize: Proptosis, tense periorbital swelling, chemosis, a hard globe on palpation, pain, reduced vision or colour vision, afferent pupillary defect, raised intraocular pressure.
hazards.rescue: Stop surgery, remove packing, call ophthalmology. Rapid or arterial hematoma (tense orbit and proptosis with falling vision, a new afferent pupillary defect, or intraocular pressure above about 40 mmHg): immediate lateral canthotomy with inferior cantholysis at the table or bedside, without waiting for imaging or the ophthalmologist; the lower lid should then distract freely — recheck vision and pressure, and add superior cantholysis if still tight. If the orbit stays tight, endoscopic medial orbital decompression with periorbital incision, controlling the ethmoidal artery if it is the source. Medical adjuncts (osmotic agents, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, steroids) only alongside. Slow venous hematoma: close observation, head up; massage is controversial.

hazards.name: PEA injury
hazards.site: Posterior ethmoid roof just anterior to the sphenoid face.
hazards.mechanism: Removing the last posterior ethmoid partitions at the skull base with a debrider or forceps.
hazards.consequence: Bleeding (usually modest, heavier when the artery is enlarged by an anterior skull-base tumor or after SPA ligation), orbital hematoma if the stump retracts, and a view obscured right next to the optic canal.
hazards.prevent: Expect it a few millimetres anterior to the sphenoid face; keep instruments below and in front of it; coagulate with bipolar before dividing it in extended approaches.
hazards.recognize: Bleeding from a transverse ridge on the posterior roof; orbital signs if it retracts.
hazards.rescue: Bipolar under vision or warm irrigation and pressure; do not blindly cauterize near the optic canal; manage orbital signs as orbital hematoma.

hazards.name: Lamina papyracea breach with fat exposure
hazards.site: Anywhere along the lamina; commonly at the bulla, the basal lamella's lateral attachment, or a pre-existing dehiscence.
hazards.mechanism: Lateral pressure through a thin or dehiscent lamina, often while removing the bulla or during uncinectomy/antrostomy; then fat is mistaken for polyp.
hazards.consequence: Orbital fat in the field, periorbital emphysema with nose blowing, orbital hematoma, and a pathway for the debrider to reach the medial rectus.
hazards.prevent: Identify the lamina early and keep it in view; CT for dehiscence; ballottement test; no powered tools facing the lamina.
hazards.recognize: Yellow fat lobules that move with globe pressure and float in saline; bruising or crepitus of the lids after surgery.
hazards.rescue: Stop powered instruments there; do not remove the fat; finish the dissection away from it with cold instruments; avoid tight packing, advise no nose blowing; check eye movements and vision on waking.

hazards.name: Medial rectus injury
hazards.site: Mid and posterior lamina, where the muscle lies nearly on the bone.
hazards.mechanism: A microdebrider through a lamina breach suctions fat and then muscle; less often a forceps grasping periorbita. In optic nerve decompression, a sheath incision carried forward through the [[s.annulus-of-zinn|annulus of Zinn]], where the rectus muscles arise.
hazards.consequence: Transection, contusion or entrapment with severe, often permanent diplopia; muscle fragments in the specimen.
hazards.prevent: No powered instruments near a breached lamina; recognize fat early; in decompression, incise periorbita in strips with a sickle blade rather than with a debrider. Keep an optic sheath incision superomedial and short of the rectus origins.
hazards.recognize: Muscle in the debrider trap or specimen; postoperative diplopia with limited adduction (or restriction on forced duction).
hazards.rescue: Urgent ophthalmology/strabismus assessment and MRI; early exploration and repair when transected; later strabismus surgery.

hazards.name: Optic nerve injury in an Onodi cell
hazards.site: Lateral or superior wall of a sphenoethmoidal (Onodi) cell, or the posterior lamina at the orbital apex.
hazards.mechanism: The Onodi cell is mistaken for the sphenoid and its lateral wall removed or crushed; thermal injury from cautery near the canal.
hazards.consequence: Immediate, usually irreversible visual loss.
hazards.prevent: CLOSE review for an Onodi cell and optic dehiscence; open the true sphenoid medially and inferiorly first; never remove the lateral wall of the last posterior ethmoid cell; avoid monopolar and heat near the canal.
hazards.recognize: Visual loss or afferent pupillary defect on waking; CT shows the fractured canal wall.
hazards.rescue: Emergency ophthalmology; CT; options (optic canal decompression, steroids) have limited evidence — prevention is everything.

hazards.name: Intracranial penetration through the ethmoid roof
hazards.site: Ethmoid roof, often posteriorly where it slopes lower than expected, or at a skull-base cell mistaken for an ethmoid partition.
hazards.mechanism: Instruments angled horizontally or upward in the posterior ethmoid, or a debrider running along the roof, pass through the fovea into the frontal lobe.
hazards.consequence: CSF leak, pneumocephalus, frontal lobe contusion or hemorrhage, injury to anterior cerebral artery branches, meningitis, abscess.
hazards.prevent: Find the roof posteriorly and follow it forward; respect the downward slope; see behind each partition; use navigation in revision or distorted anatomy.
hazards.recognize: CSF or brain tissue in the field, sudden brisk bleeding from above; postoperative neurological change or leak.
hazards.rescue: Stop, do not pull out tissue from above, control bleeding with gentle packing, urgent CT/CTA and neurosurgery; repair the defect as for CSF leak once stable.

hazards.name: Cribriform fracture from middle turbinate avulsion
hazards.site: The MT's vertical skull-base attachment at the cribriform/lateral lamella junction.
hazards.mechanism: Grasping and twisting the MT or its polyps transmits force to its skull-base attachment and fractures the cribriform plate.
hazards.consequence: CSF leak and olfactory fibre injury, often unnoticed until after surgery.
hazards.prevent: Cut MT tissue with through-cutting instruments; never twist; preserve the vertical attachment.
hazards.recognize: Clear fluid from the olfactory cleft side; postoperative unilateral rhinorrhea.
hazards.rescue: Endoscopic repair of the defect with graft; see [[p.csf-leak-repair]].

hazards.name: Frontal recess scarring and stenosis
hazards.site: Frontal recess and ostium.
hazards.mechanism: Circumferential mucosal stripping (including trimming around an outflow just widened by a balloon), exposed or osteitic bone, retained cell walls, lateralized MT, or fat prolapse narrowing the outflow.
hazards.consequence: Iatrogenic frontal sinusitis or mucocele years later; with retained cells ([[h.retained-frontal-cells]]), a leading cause of revision frontal surgery.
hazards.prevent: Uncap cells instead of stripping ([[pr.uncap-the-egg]]); preserve and stabilize the MT; leave no bone bare around the full circumference; consider mucosal flaps or stents in narrow recesses; careful postoperative debridement.
hazards.recognize: Recurrent frontal pain and opacification; endoscopic synechiae or MT adhesion; CT shows neo-osteogenesis at the recess.
hazards.rescue: Early: lyse adhesions and medialize the MT in clinic; late: revision frontal sinusotomy, escalating to Draf IIb/III.

hazards.name: Retained frontal recess cells or uncinate remnant
hazards.site: Upper uncinate, agger nasi roof, the dome of a supra agger frontal cell or suprabullar frontal cell inside the sinus, a supraorbital ethmoid cell opened instead of the sinus.
hazards.mechanism: The surgeon opens a cell and believes it is the frontal sinus, or clears only the lower recess because the cell's dome is out of view without a 70° scope.
hazards.consequence: Persistent or recurrent frontal sinusitis despite 'frontal surgery'; the most common anatomic finding in revision frontal cases.
hazards.prevent: Build the recess on CT and name every cell; confirm entry to the true sinus (posterior table, intersinus septum, sinus roof seen, navigation); use angled scopes and instruments.
hazards.recognize: On review CT, a residual cell wall or uncinate in the recess; endoscopically a blind-ending cavity.
hazards.rescue: Revision with the cells removed under angled vision; Draf IIa or wider as needed.

hazards.name: Iatrogenic smell loss
hazards.site: Olfactory cleft, upper septum, MT medial surface, cribriform plate.
hazards.mechanism: Stripping cleft mucosa, resecting or avulsing the MT, drilling behind the first olfactory fibre, or planned resection of the cribriform plate and bulbs.
hazards.consequence: Hyposmia or anosmia, often permanent; transcribriform resection makes it certain on the resected side.
hazards.prevent: Leave cleft mucosa alone; cut rather than tear near the cleft; respect the first olfactory fibre in Draf III; counsel patients before transcribriform surgery and preserve one side when oncologically safe.
hazards.recognize: Patient-reported and tested smell loss after surgery; distinguish from edema or crusting early.
hazards.rescue: Clear crusts and treat inflammation; olfactory training; counselling. No surgical rescue for sectioned fila.

hazards.name: Cribriform injury during Draf III
hazards.site: Behind the frontal T, where the posterior frontal floor meets the olfactory fossa on each side of the septum.
hazards.mechanism: Drilling posteriorly instead of anteriorly and laterally, or removing too much posterior-superior septum.
hazards.consequence: CSF leak and anosmia.
hazards.prevent: Identify the first olfactory fibre on each side before widening; keep the drill anterior to the frontal T; take bone forward (beak) and laterally.
hazards.recognize: Clear fluid at the posterior margin; exposed dura.
hazards.rescue: Repair immediately with a free mucosal or fascia graft; review packing and postoperative care accordingly.

hazards.name: Frontal neo-ostium restenosis
hazards.site: The drilled frontal ostium or common frontal cavity.
hazards.mechanism: Circumferential exposed bone heals with scar and new bone; a small initial opening and persistent inflammation accelerate it.
hazards.consequence: Recurrent frontal obstruction; revision surgery.
hazards.prevent: Make the opening as large as the anatomy allows; cover bare bone with mucosal flaps or free grafts; control inflammatory disease medically; close follow-up and debridement.
hazards.recognize: Progressive narrowing on endoscopy, most of it in the first year ([[m.draf-iii-ostium-narrowing]]).
hazards.rescue: In-office debridement and steroid therapy early; a thick fibrotic web on the front of the beak at about 12 weeks can be injected with triamcinolone (0.3–0.5 mL of 40 mg/mL through a long 25G needle); revision drill-out with mucosal grafting if it closes.

hazards.name: Frontal posterior table breach
hazards.site: Posterior table, especially inferiorly where it becomes skull base, or anywhere in a small or shallow sinus.
hazards.mechanism: Drilling posteriorly in a narrow AP sinus, a trephine placed too high or too far from the midline over a small sinus, or an osteotome angled posteriorly when cutting an osteoplastic flap. A balloon inflated in a frontal outflow narrowed by anterior osteitis or an osteoma can transmit its force to the posterior table.
hazards.consequence: CSF leak, frontal lobe injury, meningitis, pneumocephalus.
hazards.prevent: Measure AP depth on sagittal CT; identify the posterior table first and drill anteriorly; trephinate where CT shows the sinus is deepest; bevel flap cuts toward the sinus using a CT- or navigation-based template. Before balloon dilation, check the CT for osteitis or an osteoma narrowing the outflow, and open such an outflow conventionally instead.
hazards.recognize: Clear fluid, visible dura or brain; postoperative rhinorrhea or neurological change.
hazards.rescue: Repair with graft (underlay/overlay) endoscopically or through the open approach; neurosurgical input for brain or dural injury.

hazards.name: Supraorbital/supratrochlear nerve injury
hazards.site: Supraorbital notch and medial brow.
hazards.mechanism: Brow incision or periosteal elevation cuts or stretches the nerves.
hazards.consequence: Numbness or dysesthesia of the forehead and scalp back to the vertex.
hazards.prevent: Palpate the notch; keep the trephination incision medial to it and deepen bluntly; elevate subperiosteally with the nerves in the flap.
hazards.recognize: Postoperative forehead numbness.
hazards.rescue: Usually partial recovery over months; counselling.

hazards.name: Osteoplastic flap cut outside the sinus
hazards.site: Margins of the anterior table outline.
hazards.mechanism: An inaccurate template (plain film magnification, no navigation) or osteotome angled away from the sinus.
hazards.consequence: Entry into the anterior cranial fossa or orbit; fractured flap; contour deformity.
hazards.prevent: Use a navigation- or CT-derived template; bevel cuts toward the sinus; small initial cuts to confirm the sinus margin.
hazards.recognize: Dura or orbital fat at the cut; flap that will not hinge.
hazards.rescue: Repair dura; plate and fix the fragmented flap; manage contour later.

hazards.name: Late mucocele after frontal obliteration
hazards.site: Obliterated frontal sinus.
hazards.mechanism: Residual mucosa left in the sinus or recess (especially in bony crevices) keeps secreting behind the obliteration material. Posterior table erosion can mean mucosa already sits on dura, where it cannot be removed completely.
hazards.consequence: Mucocele years later, possibly with orbital or intracranial extension, hard to image against fat graft.
hazards.prevent: Remove every trace of mucosa and burr the inner cortex; plug the recess; consider endoscopic Draf III instead of obliteration when feasible.
hazards.recognize: Recurrent swelling, pain, globe displacement; MRI is the best follow-up study, but it can miss small mucoceles and cannot reliably tell viable fat from oil cysts of fat necrosis or granulation tissue.
hazards.rescue: Endoscopic marsupialization (often via Draf III) or revision open surgery.

hazards.name: New diplopia after orbital decompression
hazards.site: Medial wall and floor, inferomedial strut.
hazards.mechanism: Unbalanced prolapse of orbital contents inferomedially after strut and floor removal changes muscle vectors.
hazards.consequence: New or worsened strabismus requiring prisms or strabismus surgery.
hazards.prevent: Preserve the inferomedial strut when proptosis reduction needs allow; balanced (medial plus lateral) decompression; periorbital incisions planned to control prolapse.
hazards.recognize: Postoperative diplopia, especially in primary and down-gaze. New diplopia is reported in up to a third of patients and is often temporary.
hazards.rescue: Observation for resolution, prisms, then strabismus surgery once stable — usually not before 8–10 months after decompression.

hazards.name: Frontal recess obstruction by prolapsed orbital fat
hazards.site: Upper lamina and frontal recess.
hazards.mechanism: Removing the lamina up to the skull base anteriorly and incising the periorbita there lets fat prolapse into the frontal recess.
hazards.consequence: Iatrogenic frontal sinusitis or mucocele.
hazards.prevent: Clear the frontal recess first; leave the uppermost anterior lamina (the frontal recess's lateral wall) or avoid periorbital incisions there.
hazards.recognize: Frontal opacification on postoperative CT; frontal pain.
hazards.rescue: Frontal sinusotomy (Draf IIa or more) to re-establish drainage.

hazards.name: Infraorbital nerve injury during floor decompression
hazards.site: Orbital floor medial to and at the infraorbital canal.
hazards.mechanism: Floor removal carried lateral to the canal or fracturing the canal.
hazards.consequence: Cheek and upper lip numbness.
hazards.prevent: Remove floor only medial to the canal from an endoscopic approach.
hazards.recognize: Postoperative V2 numbness.
hazards.rescue: Observation; usually improves.

hazards.name: Trochlea detachment
hazards.site: Superomedial orbital rim.
hazards.mechanism: Supraperiosteal dissection or cutting through the periosteum at the trochlear fossa during Lynch-type incisions or trephination.
hazards.consequence: Superior oblique dysfunction and vertical-torsional diplopia.
hazards.prevent: Stay strictly subperiosteal so the trochlea stays attached to the periosteum and resuspends; close periosteum accurately.
hazards.recognize: Diplopia on down- and in-gaze after external medial approaches.
hazards.rescue: Usually resolves with time if periosteum was intact; strabismus assessment if persistent.

hazards.name: Medial canthal tendon disruption (telecanthus)
hazards.site: Medial canthus and lacrimal crest.
hazards.mechanism: External (Lynch) incision placed too low or elevation that detaches the tendon from the lacrimal crest without repair.
hazards.consequence: Telecanthus, rounding of the medial canthus, epiphora.
hazards.prevent: Keep the incision above the tendon; if detached, tag and reattach (transnasal wiring or plate) at closure.
hazards.recognize: Widened intercanthal distance postoperatively.
hazards.rescue: Canthopexy.

hazards.name: Frontopolar/orbitofrontal artery injury
hazards.site: Superior-posterior capsule of olfactory-groove tumors, gyrus rectus surface.
hazards.mechanism: Coagulating or tearing vessels adherent to the tumor capsule during extracapsular dissection.
hazards.consequence: Frontal infarction, intracerebral hemorrhage.
hazards.prevent: Debulk centrally, then dissect the capsule off the arachnoid with vessels kept on the brain side; identify them on CTA/MRI preoperatively.
hazards.recognize: Arterial bleeding from above the tumor; postoperative neurological change or infarct on imaging.
hazards.rescue: Bipolar the bleeding point with low power, hemostatic agents, neurosurgical control; ICU observation.

hazards.name: Failed anterior skull-base repair
hazards.site: Cribriform, lateral lamella, ethmoid roof or frontal sinus posterior wall defects.
hazards.mechanism: Graft displacement, incomplete mucosal removal around the defect, missed second defect, or untreated raised intracranial pressure (spontaneous leaks).
hazards.consequence: Persistent or recurrent CSF rhinorrhea, meningitis.
hazards.prevent: Localize every defect (thin CT, intrathecal fluorescein where used); denude the margin; multilayer repair; identify and treat idiopathic intracranial hypertension (obesity, empty sella, venous sinus stenosis).
hazards.recognize: Recurrent clear rhinorrhea; beta-2 transferrin positive.
hazards.rescue: Re-image, revise with larger or vascularized reconstruction, treat intracranial pressure (acetazolamide, shunt, venous stenting as indicated).

hazards.name: Bleeding during encephalocele reduction
hazards.site: Encephalocele stalk at the skull-base defect.
hazards.mechanism: Pulling or avulsing the sac tears vessels in its stalk, which can retract intracranially.
hazards.consequence: Intracranial hemorrhage.
hazards.prevent: Reduce the herniated tissue with bipolar cautery down to the level of the skull base, never by traction; cut rather than tear.
hazards.recognize: Bleeding retracting up through the defect.
hazards.rescue: Bipolar at the defect, gentle packing, urgent CT, neurosurgery.

hazards.name: Incomplete drainage of an orbital subperiosteal abscess
hazards.site: Superior, superolateral or loculated abscesses; orbital (intraperiorbital) collections.
hazards.mechanism: An endoscopic medial approach reaches only medial collections; loculations and bleeding inflamed mucosa hide the rest.
hazards.consequence: Persisting orbital pressure, visual loss, spread to orbital abscess or cavernous sinus.
hazards.prevent: Read the contrast CT for the abscess's position; plan an external (superior/Lynch) route for superior or lateral collections; remove the lamina widely over the abscess.
hazards.recognize: No improvement or worsening vision, motility or proptosis within 24–48 hours; repeat CT.
hazards.rescue: Repeat imaging and drainage through the appropriate external route; ophthalmology co-management.

principles.name: Find the skull base posteriorly, then work anteriorly
principles.rule: Dissect along the lamina papyracea from front to back, identify the skull base in the posterior ethmoid (or sphenoid), then clear the roof from posterior to anterior.
principles.why: Posteriorly the cells are large and the roof broad and easy to recognize; anteriorly the roof is thin, obscured by cells and bounded by the lateral lamella and AEA. Working forward along an already-seen roof lets you remove partitions without pushing into an unseen one.
principles.caveat: In a small or heavily diseased posterior ethmoid, use the sphenoid roof (entered medially and low) instead; image guidance does not replace this sequence.

principles.name: Use the medial orbital floor as the height reference (Casiano)
principles.rule: Make a wide maxillary antrostomy, identify the medial orbital floor, and enter the posterior ethmoid and sphenoid at or just above that height, medial to the lamina; the skull base is always above it.
principles.why: The orbital floor is constant and visible even when the ethmoid is distorted by polyps or prior surgery, so it fixes a safe vertical level for going posteriorly; Casiano's distances to the skull base and sphenoid come from cadaver measurements (11 heads, 18 sides), not a clinical outcome series.
principles.caveat: The skull base lies closer to the orbital floor in some patients (low roof); confirm the vertical distance on sagittal CT before relying on it. A tall, well-pneumatized maxillary sinus with a short posterior ethmoid (maxillary-to-posterior-ethmoid height ratio above about 2:1) is the pattern that leads toward the skull base instead of the sphenoid.

principles.name: At the ethmoid roof, stay lateral
principles.rule: Along the skull base, dissect toward the lamina papyracea, not along the middle turbinate's vertical attachment; never push or twist medially at the roof.
principles.why: The medial roof is the lateral lamella and cribriform plate — the thinnest bone of the skull base; the lateral fovea is thicker and has the orbit (which you can see) beside it.
principles.caveat: A flat lateral lamella ([[c.gera]] class III) extends laterally, so the 'lateral' roof may still be lamella; read the coronal CT.

principles.name: The AEA is the posterior limit of the frontal recess
principles.rule: Frontal recess dissection happens anterior to the AEA; locate the artery on CT (orbital notch, sagittal position) and see it before clearing the posterior wall of the recess.
principles.why: The frontal ostium lies anterior to the artery — in latex-injected cadavers it ran between the bullar and basal lamellae on every side, about 11 mm (6–15 mm) behind the posterior wall of the frontal recess — so there is nothing to gain behind it and everything to lose — orbital hematoma and skull-base injury.
principles.caveat: A supraorbital ethmoid cell or suprabullar frontal cell can put air (and the artery) anterior to where you expect; follow the pathway, not the rule.

principles.name: CLOSE: the preoperative sinus CT checklist
principles.rule: Before every FESS review the CT for: C — Cribriform plate (Keros depth, asymmetry, lateral lamella); L — Lamina papyracea (dehiscence, fat herniation); O — Onodi cell (optic nerve in its wall); S — Sphenoid sinus (pneumatization, septa inserting on the ICA, optic/ICA dehiscence); E — (anterior) Ethmoidal artery (canal in a mesentery, relation to cells).
principles.why: These five findings account for the preventable catastrophes of sinus surgery; saying them aloud before incision turns them into expected findings.
principles.caveat: It is a minimum, not a full read: also build the frontal recess ([[pr.frontal-building-blocks]]) and note maxillary, uncinate and septal anatomy.

principles.name: Build the frontal recess in three planes before surgery
principles.rule: On triplanar CT, identify each frontal recess cell in coronal, sagittal and axial views, name it (IFAC), and draw the drainage pathway around the cells from the ostium to the middle meatus; operate to that plan.
principles.why: The recess is a 3D puzzle that no single plane shows; knowing which side of each cell the pathway runs tells you which wall to remove first and where the sinus really is.

principles.name: Uncap the egg; preserve frontal recess mucosa
principles.rule: Enter frontal recess cells from below, then fracture their caps (thin roofs) upward and away from the drainage pathway and remove the loose fragments with through-cutting instruments; do not strip mucosa, and never leave bone bare around the whole circumference.
principles.why: Circumferential mucosal loss and osteitic bone cause concentric scarring and restenosis of the frontal outflow; preserved mucosa keeps mucociliary clearance.

principles.name: Enter the basal lamella low and medial
principles.rule: Open the posterior ethmoid through the basal lamella inferomedially, just above its horizontal part and lateral to the MT, then extend the opening laterally and superiorly under vision.
principles.why: That point is farthest from both the skull base and the lamina papyracea and it preserves the MT's stability.

principles.name: Press the globe, watch the lamina
principles.rule: Keep the eyes uncovered in the field; before and during ethmoid dissection press gently on the closed eye while watching the lamina endoscopically. Movement of the wall or of fat means a dehiscence or breach.
principles.why: It finds a dehiscent lamina before a debrider does, and confirms a suspected breach intraoperatively.

principles.name: Never remove a partition you cannot see behind
principles.rule: Before cutting a bony partition near the skull base or orbit, pass a probe or curette behind it into air, confirm the space on CT or navigation, then remove it with a movement away from the skull base or orbit.
principles.why: Most skull-base and orbital injuries happen when a partition is removed blindly and turns out to be the roof or the lamina.

principles.name: Match the extent of frontal surgery to the disease
principles.rule: Choose the least extensive frontal procedure that removes the obstructing cells and treats the pathology (EFSS grade or Draf type), and escalate to Draf IIb/III when anatomy or disease makes a lesser opening fail.
principles.why: Every extra millimetre of drilled bone risks osteitis and scarring, but an undersized opening in recalcitrant or neoplastic disease fails; the grade is decided by CT anatomy and disease, not habit.

principles.name: The first olfactory fibre is the posterior limit of a Draf III
principles.rule: In a Draf III, identify the first olfactory fibre on each side of the septal window and keep all drilling anterior to the line joining them (the frontal T); take the bone forward (beak) and laterally, not backward.
principles.why: Behind that line is the cribriform plate: drilling there causes CSF leak and anosmia.

principles.name: Preserve and stabilize the middle turbinate
principles.rule: Keep the MT's vertical skull-base attachment and the horizontal basal lamella intact; resect only diseased or obstructing parts, and medialize or suture the MT if it becomes unstable.
principles.why: A lateralized MT scars against the lamina and closes the frontal recess; avulsing it fractures the cribriform plate.
principles.caveat: In extended approaches or with extensive polyposis, partial MT resection may be justified — then protect the frontal recess from the remnant.

procedures.name: Anterior ethmoidectomy
indications: Chronic rhinosinusitis with anterior ethmoid disease after appropriate medical therapy
Access to the frontal recess, lamina papyracea or anterior skull base
Recurrent acute or complicated sinusitis with ethmoid involvement
procedures.corridor: Middle meatus lateral to the MT, after uncinectomy and maxillary antrostomy.

preop.check: Keros depth, Gera angle and roof asymmetry on coronal CT
preop.why: Predicts where the medial roof is weakest and how far the lateral lamella extends.

preop.check: Lamina papyracea integrity and fat herniation
preop.why: A dehiscence changes where powered instruments may go.

preop.check: AEA position: orbital notch, canal in the roof or in a mesentery, supraorbital ethmoid cell
preop.why: A hanging artery at the back of the frontal recess is the usual cause of orbital hematoma.

preop.check: Bulla size and pneumatization, bullar lamella reaching the skull base
preop.why: Defines the posterior wall of the frontal recess and whether a suprabullar recess exists.

preop.check: MT anatomy (concha bullosa, paradoxical curve) and uncinate attachment
preop.why: Decides access and where the frontal sinus drains.

steps.do: Medialize the MT gently; complete the uncinectomy and a maxillary antrostomy wide enough to see the orbital floor.
steps.think: Is the plane of the lamina defined above the antrostomy? Do I have the medial orbital floor as a height reference?

steps.do: Enter the bulla inferomedially with a curette or straight forceps and remove its anterior and medial walls.
steps.think: Is this a pneumatized bulla or a solid torus lateralis? Enter low and medial — never up through the roof.

steps.do: Take the lateral bulla wall to the lamina papyracea; ballot the globe while watching the wall.
steps.think: Does the wall move with globe pressure? If fat appears, switch to cold instruments and work away from it.

steps.do: Identify the basal lamella behind the retrobullar recess.
steps.think: Is disease behind it on CT? If so, continue as [[p.posterior-ethmoidectomy]] and return to the roof from behind.

steps.do: With a 30° scope, clear suprabullar cells and the bullar lamella up to the skull base, from posterior to anterior, after locating the AEA.
steps.think: Is the AEA in the roof or hanging? Is this partition a cell wall or the roof itself — can I get a probe behind it?

steps.do: Preserve the MT's vertical attachment; trim only obstructing or diseased MT with through-cutting instruments.
steps.think: Will the MT stay medial? If unstable, plan medialization (suture or controlled synechia).

endpoints: Anterior ethmoid cells removed from the lamina papyracea to the MT and up to a smooth skull base
Basal lamella identified
AEA seen and preserved
Frontal recess addressed as planned ([[p.draf-i]])
pitfalls: Opening the bulla by pushing through its roof
Mistaking a torus lateralis or the basal lamella for the lamina papyracea
Stripping mucosa from the skull base and frontal recess
Debriding medially along the MT attachment

procedures.name: Posterior ethmoidectomy
indications: Chronic rhinosinusitis or polyposis involving the posterior ethmoid
Access to the sphenoid, orbital apex, optic canal or posterior anterior skull base
procedures.corridor: Through the basal lamella, lateral to the MT and superior turbinate.

preop.check: Sphenoethmoidal (Onodi) cell and optic nerve position
preop.why: The last posterior ethmoid cell may carry the optic nerve in its wall.

preop.check: Skull-base height above the orbital floor on sagittal/coronal CT
preop.why: Tells you how much vertical room there is (Casiano reference).

preop.check: PEA and sphenoid face position; optic/ICA dehiscence in the sphenoid
preop.why: Warns where the dissection must slow down.

steps.do: Perforate the basal lamella inferomedially at the junction of its vertical and horizontal parts.
steps.think: Am I above the horizontal part, lateral to the MT, and at or just above the medial orbital floor height?

steps.do: Enlarge the opening laterally to the lamina and upward, removing posterior ethmoid partitions.
steps.think: The medial rectus is closest here — cold instruments against the lamina.

steps.do: Identify the skull base in the largest posterior ethmoid cell, or open the sphenoid medially and inferiorly and use its roof ([[p.sphenoidotomy]]).
steps.think: Is this last cell an Onodi cell (horizontal septum on coronal CT)? Where is the optic nerve? Never take the lateral wall of the last cell blindly.

steps.do: Clear the skull base from posterior to anterior with 0° and 30° scopes, taking partitions down and away from the roof, forward to the AEA.
steps.think: Follow the slope: the roof rises toward the front. Probe behind every partition before removing it.

steps.do: Check MT stability, preserve the horizontal basal lamella, and medialize the MT if needed.
steps.think: Will this cavity stay open and the MT stay medial through healing?

endpoints: Posterior ethmoid partitions removed from lamina to MT/superior turbinate up to a smooth skull base
Sphenoid face and PEA identified
MT stable
pitfalls: Entering the posterior ethmoid high and lateral
Mistaking an Onodi cell for the sphenoid
Horizontal instrument angles in the posterior ethmoid where the roof is lower

procedures.name: Revision FESS: completion sphenoethmoidectomy
indications: Persistent chronic rhinosinusitis after limited surgery (antrostomy and partial ethmoidectomy), aiming to make this the last operation — usually with frontal recess dissection
Retained osteitic partitions along the lamina papyracea and skull base keeping the overlying mucosa inflamed
procedures.corridor: Through the scarred middle meatus along the lamina papyracea to the sphenoid, then forward along the skull base.

preop.check: Residual partitions, osteitis and neo-osteogenesis along the lamina and skull base
preop.why: They are the usual nidus of persistent disease and the targets of the revision.

preop.check: Maxillary sinus height against posterior ethmoid height on coronal CT
preop.why: A tall, well-pneumatized maxillary sinus with a short posterior ethmoid (height ratio above about 2:1) draws the surgeon toward the skull base instead of the sphenoid — a CSF leak pattern.

preop.check: Repeat the [[pr.close-ct-review]] for the altered anatomy
preop.why: Landmarks removed at the first operation (uncinate, bulla, part of the MT) can no longer be relied on.

preop.check: Inflammatory load
preop.why: A preoperative oral steroid course may reduce both difficulty and blood loss in polyp disease.

steps.do: Debulk polyps with the microdebrider, but take bone with hand instruments, which give better feel in thick osteitic bone.
steps.think: Soft tissue with the debrider, bone by feel.

steps.do: Revise the maxillary antrostomy: remove the uncinate remnant with a backbiter, and take the posterior fontanelle and posterior maxillary partitions back to the posterior maxillary wall with through-cutting forceps.
steps.think: A posterior pocket left behind acts as an air scoop and a persistent osteitic nidus. The medial orbital floor is my height reference ([[pr.casiano-medial-orbital-floor]]).

steps.do: Find the sphenoid through the posterior ethmoid at or just above the orbital-floor height, medially. Clues in distorted anatomy: the last posterior ethmoid cell is pyramid-shaped where the superior turbinate's basal lamella meets the skull base, and the posterior maxillary wall curves back toward the sphenoid face.
steps.think: Am I heading for the sphenoid or up into the skull base? With a short posterior ethmoid, stay low and medial.

steps.do: Enlarge the sphenoidotomy widely; before taking bone inferiorly with a Kerrison, retract the mucosa with a Freer to protect the septal branch of the sphenopalatine artery. A maximal opening lets retained allergic mucin be cleared and the sphenoid irrigated.
steps.think: Is the opening big enough for the patient to irrigate it?

steps.do: Clear the skull base from posterior to anterior, taking each partition down and away while erring laterally against the skeletonized lamina papyracea; the curve of the orbital floor continues into the medial orbital wall and predicts its contour.
steps.think: The roof slopes down toward the midline. Can I feel behind this partition and see in front of it ([[pr.see-behind-before-cut]])? Skull base is usually thicker and ivory-white — but osteitis blurs that difference.

steps.do: Last, remove the superior uncinate remnant on the anteromedial orbital wall and complete the frontal recess dissection as planned ([[p.draf-i]] or beyond).
steps.think: Easy to overlook after working posteriorly — a retained upper uncinate keeps the frontal recess obstructed.

steps.do: Finish without packing where possible, and tell the patient not to blow the nose.
steps.think: Most revision cases need no packing or hemostatic agent (87% of 165 patients in one series); spacers reduce synechiae without a clear bleeding benefit. Nose-blowing after an unrecognized lamina breach causes orbital or subcutaneous emphysema.

endpoints: Smooth skull base and lamina papyracea from the sphenoid to the frontal recess, with no retained partitions
Wide maxillary antrostomy including the posterior fontanelle
Wide sphenoidotomy
Upper uncinate remnant removed and the frontal recess open
pitfalls: Powered instruments on osteitic bone at the skull base
Mistaking the skull base for a septation in a short posterior ethmoid
Leaving the upper uncinate remnant or a posterior maxillary pocket

procedures.name: Postoperative endoscopic debridement after sinus surgery
indications: Routine follow-up after FESS: clearing crust, clot, retained bone fragments and early synechiae while the cavity heals
More frequent visits after operations that crust more — Draf III drill-out, medial maxillectomy, extended skull-base surgery
procedures.corridor: In clinic, under topical anesthesia and decongestion, with 0° and angled endoscopes through the operated cavity.

preop.check: What was done, and what must not be disturbed
preop.why: After a CSF leak repair or skull-base tumor resection, debride minimally near the reconstruction; after orbital surgery, leave the orbitotomy alone for the first weeks.

preop.check: Will the patient tolerate it?
preop.why: Many children cannot tolerate office debridement and need it under anesthesia.

steps.do: Schedule: first visit about 5–7 days after surgery, the second at 1–2 weeks and a third around 4–5 weeks when the cavity is nearly healed. Anesthetize and decongest topically (e.g. 4% cocaine); analgesia before the first visit helps.
steps.think: Is this cavity healing as expected, or does it need more frequent visits?

steps.do: Work in a fixed order: nasal cavity and nasopharynx, then the sphenoid face as the posterior limit, then along the lamina papyracea and skull base, then the maxillary sinus, and the frontal recess last. Keep instruments along the lateral wall, away from the sensitive septal mucosa.
steps.think: Am I lifting crust off healing mucosa, or tearing the mucosa itself?

steps.do: Leave crust at or near the sphenopalatine foramen, and over a resected MT stump, alone for at least the first 10 days.
steps.think: An adherent crust pulled here can start an arterial bleed in the clinic.

steps.do: Frontal recess: find and clear it with a 30°/45° view (a Silastic stent left at surgery makes the natural recess easy to find); divide early synechiae and adhesions of the MT.
steps.think: Is the pathway open, and is the MT staying medial?

steps.do: Between visits: high-volume isotonic saline irrigation from 24–48 hours after surgery; steroid (e.g. budesonide) irrigation for polyp disease where prescribed; anti-staphylococcal antibiotic cover while splints, spacers or packing remain.
steps.think: Retained packing or splints carry a toxic shock risk — cover them and take them out on time.

endpoints: Cavity free of obstructing crust and clot
Synechiae divided and the MT medial
Openings patent as healing completes
pitfalls: Vigorous debridement over a skull-base repair
Pulling crust off the sphenopalatine region in the first 10 days
Instruments dragged along the septum
Treating an arterial bleed with silver nitrate: it needs electrocautery, and repacking or a return to theatre if uncontrolled
Not being ready for a vasovagal reaction: stop, lay the patient flat with the legs raised, cold pack and fluids

procedures.name: Draf I frontal sinusotomy (frontal recess clearance)
indications: Frontal recess obstruction by cells with a normal frontal ostium
Frontal sinus disease expected to resolve once the recess is cleared
procedures.corridor: Middle meatus above the MT axilla, anterior to the bulla and AEA, lateral to the MT vertical lamella.

preop.check: Build the frontal recess on triplanar CT and name every IFAC cell
preop.why: The pathway runs around the cells; its side of each cell decides which wall you remove.

preop.check: Uncinate superior attachment
preop.why: Lamina insertion (terminal recess) — sinus drains medial to it; skull-base/MT insertion — drains into the infundibulum and the upper uncinate must go.

preop.check: AEA position and supraorbital ethmoid cell
preop.why: The posterior limit of the dissection.

preop.check: AP diameter of the frontal recess on sagittal CT
preop.why: The best single predictor of how hard the dissection will be: a narrow recess tolerates little instrumentation and is easily stripped of mucosa; some surgeons dilate it with a balloon before using instruments.

steps.do: Set up: in a full FESS leave the frontal recess for last, after the antrostomy, sphenoethmoidectomy and identification of the skull base. Head up about 30°, inject at least 2 mL of lidocaine with adrenaline at the MT axilla, and keep 1:1000 adrenaline pledgets for the field.
steps.think: Is the skull base already identified behind, and is the field dry enough to work above the axilla?

steps.do: Remove the upper uncinate up to its attachment, recognising a terminal recess if present.
steps.think: Where does the uncinate attach? A blind-ending terminal recess is not the frontal ostium.

steps.do: Enter the agger nasi cell from behind/below (or via an axillary flap) and uncap its roof, fracturing it forward and up.
steps.think: Is the pathway medial/posterior to this cell as on CT? Probe it first.

steps.do: Pass a curved probe along the drainage pathway into the sinus as planned on CT.
steps.think: Did the probe go up anterior to the skull base and AEA, and does navigation or a 70° view confirm the sinus?

steps.do: Remove supra agger and suprabullar cell caps that do not enter the sinus, fracturing them away from the pathway and removing loose fragments with through-cutting instruments.
steps.think: Mucosa of the pathway stays untouched; no bone bared around the full circumference.

steps.do: Take the bullar lamella/suprabullar recess down to the skull base, stopping at the AEA.
steps.think: Artery seen? Anything behind it is not frontal recess.

steps.do: Confirm the frontal ostium is visible and unobstructed with a 45°/70° scope; leave the ostium itself untouched.
steps.think: Is any cell wall still hanging in the ostium or dome? A cell pneumatizing through the ostium makes this EFSS grade 3 if cleared without widening the ostium, or grade 4 — a [[p.draf-iia]] — if the ostium must be enlarged.

endpoints: All cells obstructing the recess below the ostium removed
Ostium seen and probe-patent
Recess mucosa preserved; MT stable
pitfalls: Leaving the upper uncinate or agger nasi roof
Opening a supraorbital ethmoid cell and calling it the frontal sinus
Circumferential mucosal stripping
Drifting medially toward the cribriform plate with an angled scope — rotating the light post away from the midline (about 10 o'clock for a right-sided dissection) re-centres the recess

procedures.name: Draf IIa frontal sinusotomy
indications: Cells pneumatizing through the ostium into the sinus (supra agger frontal, suprabullar frontal)
Frontal mucocele
Persistent frontal disease after Draf I
Benign lesions of the frontal ostium region
procedures.corridor: Draf I corridor, then the frontal sinus floor between the lamina papyracea and the MT.

preop.check: Which cells enter the sinus and how far
preop.why: Large cells may need angled drills, curved instruments or an above-and-below approach.

preop.check: AP depth at the ostium and position of the posterior table
preop.why: Limits how much floor and beak can be removed safely.

steps.do: Complete the Draf I dissection and identify the ostium, the posterior table and the cells inside the sinus with a 70° scope.
steps.think: Where is the true sinus relative to each cell — the pathway is medial/posterior to a SAFC, anterior to a SBFC, anteromedial to a SOEC.

steps.do: Remove the walls of cells inside the sinus with curved curettes and giraffe forceps, pulling fragments down and forward.
steps.think: The SBFC's posterior wall is skull base — remove it from the front only.

steps.do: Enlarge the ostium anteriorly (beak) with a frontal sinus punch or angled drill, between the lamina papyracea and the MT.
steps.think: Preserve posterior and medial mucosa; widen forward, not backward.

steps.do: Inspect the sinus for residual cells and disease; irrigate.
steps.think: Is the opening wide enough to survive healing with the mucosa that remains?

endpoints: Frontal floor opened between lamina papyracea and MT
No cell walls remaining in the sinus
Mucosa preserved on at least part of the circumference
pitfalls: Leaving the dome of a supra agger frontal cell
Drilling posteriorly toward the skull base
Bare bone circumferentially

procedures.name: Draf IIb frontal sinusotomy
indications: Frontal disease not controlled by Draf IIa, including failed frontal surgery with neo-osteogenesis or a lateralized MT remnant
Frontal septal cell or medial disease
Benign tumors (e.g. inverted papilloma, osteoma) near the ostium
Unilateral access when a Draf III is not required
Frontal mucocele, or a previously obliterated sinus that must be reopened
Access to the posterior table for CSF leak or encephalocele repair, and selected fractures
Lateralized MT remnant obstructing the recess: the frontal sinus rescue variant — a medially based mucosal flap raised from the MT stump, a Draf IIb, then the flap laid back over the bare bone
procedures.corridor: Frontal sinus floor from the lamina papyracea to the nasal septum, including the MT's anterior skull-base attachment.

preop.check: AP depth nasal beak to posterior table
preop.why: A shallow AP depth limits the safe width of the opening. About 10 mm is often quoted as the minimum; the practical test is whether the drill fits without its shaft touching the cribriform plate or the posterior table.

preop.check: Position of the first olfactory fibre relative to the MT attachment
preop.why: The resection of the MT's anterior attachment must stay in front of it.

preop.check: Relative contraindications
preop.why: A very narrow AP diameter, severe bilateral neo-osteogenesis, disease far lateral in a well-pneumatized sinus (out of endoscopic reach — plan an above-and-below or external route), or comorbidity precluding general anesthesia.

preop.check: MRI when tumor, CSF leak, encephalocele or a previous obliteration is in question
preop.why: Separates tumor from inspissated secretions and sizes a skull-base defect; after fat obliteration it helps but is often hard to read.

steps.do: Complete a Draf IIa.
steps.think: Is the lateral part of the opening as wide as it will get before I work medially?

steps.do: Resect the anterior-superior MT attachment below the frontal floor (the lowest part of the MT can be kept for function), then drill the floor and beak medially to the septum.
steps.think: Where is the first olfactory fibre? Everything I remove medially must be anterior to it.

steps.do: Remove any frontal septal cell and smooth the opening: clear pus and bone dust, coagulate the midline soft tissue in front of the cribriform plate, trim ragged MT and septal edges, and cover exposed bone with mucosa where possible.
steps.think: Is there a mucosal edge on at least part of the circumference?

steps.do: Stabilize and dress: medialize any MT remnant with a transseptal absorbable suture; if a stent is used, prefer a thin pliable Silastic sheet to a rigid tube and remove it at about 2 weeks.
steps.think: Stents are colonized by biofilm (shown by 3 weeks, probably sooner) — the benefit must outweigh that.

endpoints: Frontal floor removed from lamina papyracea to septum on one side
Olfactory fibres untouched
pitfalls: Taking the MT attachment too far posteriorly
Leaving a medial shelf that scars shut
Trusting navigation without re-checking its registration on fixed landmarks during the case

procedures.name: Draf III / endoscopic modified Lothrop procedure
indications: Recalcitrant frontal sinusitis after prior surgery
Frontal neoplasms (e.g. inverted papilloma) needing wide access
Large or complex frontal mucoceles
Alternative to frontal obliteration
Access to the anterior skull base and frontal sinus posterior wall
procedures.corridor: Bilateral frontal floors, upper nasal septum and intersinus septum, from lamina to lamina, anterior to the first olfactory fibres.

preop.check: AP depth at the ostium (nasal beak to posterior table) on sagittal CT
preop.why: A very narrow AP depth makes the procedure hazardous or impossible; a posterior table less than 5 mm from the skin in front of the nasal beak (mostly after trauma or with craniofacial anomalies) is an absolute contraindication.

preop.check: Frontal sinus size and intersinus septum position; frontal aplasia
preop.why: Decides the shape of the common cavity.

preop.check: Posterior table dehiscence, prior CSF leak sites
preop.why: Areas to avoid drilling.

preop.check: Disease activity
preop.why: Operate when topical therapy is likely to control the airway disease; very active disease still needing systemic steroids is a relative contraindication.

preop.check: Anesthesia plan
preop.why: Total intravenous anesthesia with a low heart rate (about 55–65 bpm) and a mean arterial pressure near 60 mmHg keeps the drilling field dry (the chapter's targets; expert opinion).

steps.do: Raise the mucosal flaps first: on each side one continuous flap over the nasal beak, frontal floor, frontal process of the maxilla and the planned septal window, before any drilling.
steps.think: These flaps are what will cover the bone at the end — protect them from the drill.

steps.do: Create a window in the anterior-superior septum just below the frontal sinus floor; mark its anteroinferior corner by pushing needle-tip cautery through the septum from one side, so the flaps on both sides stay symmetric.
steps.think: Is the window high and anterior enough to let instruments cross the midline without touching the olfactory cleft?

steps.do: Identify the first olfactory fibre on each side at the posterior edge of the window.
steps.think: This line is my posterior limit for the rest of the case.

steps.do: Outside-in: on each side drill the bone lateral to the nasal beak down to the periosteum of the frontal process of the maxilla, fixing the lateral limits before the beak is opened; the periosteum shows as whiter tissue that bleeds more than bone.
steps.think: Periosteum reached on both sides? Then the lateral limits are set and the beak can come down broadly.

steps.do: Take down the beak and frontal floors between those limits on a broad inverted-U front, aiming more superiorly and anteriorly than at the recess, and open the frontal sinus mucosa as late as possible; then follow the medial orbital wall where it turns into the orbital roof to square off each side. (With a normal recess, a Draf IIa on one side can be the starting point instead — inside-out.)
steps.think: Identify the posterior table before drilling; drill forward (beak), not backward. Outside-in never depends on frontal recess anatomy, so it suits a scarred or neo-osteogenic recess better than the inside-out (Lothrop) order that starts in the recess.

steps.do: Remove the intersinus septum and any frontal septal cells to make one common cavity; smooth all edges.
steps.think: Is the frontal T clearly seen, with no bone behind it removed?

steps.do: Trim MT heads that project forward back behind the posterior edge of the septal window; cover exposed bone — above all the frontal process of the maxilla, which dries and crusts most — with the flaps and free mucosal grafts (e.g. from the posterior inferior turbinate), held by a 0.5 mm Silastic sheet cut to a template of the cavity.
steps.think: The neo-ostium will narrow substantially in the first year ([[m.draf-iii-ostium-narrowing]]); make it as large as the anatomy allows.

steps.do: Postoperative: high-volume saline irrigation from day 1; remove the Silastic at 3 weeks or later, clearing granulation, crust and unfavourable synechiae; review at about 3 and 12 weeks.
steps.think: A thick fibrotic web on the front of the beak at 12 weeks is treated early ([[h.neo-ostium-restenosis]]) before it matures.

endpoints: Common frontal opening from lamina to lamina
Posterior limit at the first olfactory fibres (frontal T)
Beak drilled to a smooth anterior curve
Bone covered where possible
pitfalls: Drilling behind the first olfactory fibre
Undersized AP opening
Leaving intersinus or septal cell remnants that scar
Boring a narrow hole toward the sinus instead of taking the beak on a broad front
Opening the inflamed frontal mucosa early — it bleeds and blinds the rest of the drilling
MT heads left in the plane of the septal window — synechiae into the olfactory cleft
Harvesting the inferior turbinate graft too deep — its artery can bleed after surgery
Expecting a Draf III alone to reach a lesion over the lateral orbital roof — it needs an added orbital transposition or an external approach

procedures.name: Frontal sinus trephination
indications: Complicated acute frontal sinusitis (orbital or intracranial spread, Pott's puffy tumor) needing drainage

A second working port (above-and-below) for disease out of endoscopic reach: far lateral cells, laterally based mucoceles or polyps, neo-osteogenic recess obstruction, benign tumors such as osteoma or inverted papilloma
Localizing the frontal ostium from above with irrigation (e.g. fluorescein-tinted saline)
Rapid decompression of both sinuses through an intersinus septectomy
Combined repair of a posterior table CSF leak or encephalocele; rarely a posterior table fracture
procedures.corridor: Medial floor of the frontal sinus (or, in a non-infected sinus, the anterior table) through a brow or upper-lid incision.

preop.check: Sinus depth and extent on CT (or navigation); aplasia or hypoplasia
preop.why: A trephine into a small sinus can enter the anterior cranial fossa.

preop.check: Supraorbital notch and supratrochlear nerve positions
preop.why: Keep the incision and dissection between/medial to them as planned.

steps.do: Mark the trephination point on CT/navigation at the medial floor where the sinus is deepest. Incision: infrabrow (most used — just under the brow, medial to the supraorbital bundle), intrabrow, suprabrow or upper-lid crease; keep it 1–2 cm and stop at the medial end of the brow.
steps.think: Is the sinus definitely behind this point? Am I medial to the supraorbital notch? Each incision trades scar visibility, brow alopecia, forehead numbness and infection. In the upper-lid route, stay preseptal above the levator and identify and retract the supraorbital and supratrochlear bundles before opening the periosteum.

steps.do: Elevate periosteum and enter through the medial floor — not so low and medial that scar reaches the frontal recess. Saucerize a window of about 6–8 mm with a 4 mm cutting bur until a blue hue shows mucosa through the last thin bone, then enter with a curette or the navigation probe; enlarge to 5–15 mm with a small Kerrison if instruments must pass.
steps.think: Angle away from the posterior table; stop as soon as I am in air or pus.

steps.do: Culture, irrigate and, if combined with endoscopy, flush dyed saline to identify the drainage pathway from below; leave a drain or cannula if needed. An 8F catheter or silicone tube sutured in place for irrigation usually comes out after 3–5 days.
steps.think: Irrigation should appear in the recess medially — if it appears somewhere unexpected, re-check the anatomy before cutting.

endpoints: Sinus drained or irrigated; pathway confirmed from below when combined
pitfalls: Trephinating a hypoplastic sinus without imaging
Lateral placement injuring the supraorbital nerve
Entering an acutely infected sinus through the anterior table — its diploic bone risks osteomyelitis and intracranial spread
A trephine placed too low and medial — scar can close the frontal recess
Trephination alone as definitive treatment for chronic inflammatory frontal disease: failure rates up to 57% are reported

procedures.name: Osteoplastic frontal sinus flap (with or without obliteration)
indications: Frontal disease inaccessible endoscopically (far lateral, supraorbital)
Selected frontal fractures, particularly those involving the frontal recess, and posterior table defects with CSF leak
Large lateral osteomas, other fibro-osseous lesions (fibrous dysplasia, ossifying fibroma) or tumors
Chronic frontal sinusitis or recurrent recess stenosis despite endoscopic surgery, including Draf III
procedures.corridor: Anterior table raised as a bone flap hinged on pericranium, via coronal or brow incision.

preop.check: Template of the sinus outline from CT or navigation
preop.why: An inaccurate outline enters the cranial cavity or orbit. Navigation outlines the sinus more accurately than a cut-out 6-foot Caldwell film or transillumination.

preop.check: Mucosal disease, posterior table integrity, outflow tract
preop.why: Decides between obliteration and a non-obliterative flap with endoscopic drainage. If the recess is undisturbed and less than about half of the mucosa is lost, the rest can be kept with endoscopic drainage; more extensive loss favors obliteration. Posterior table erosion may mean mucosa already lies on dura — obliteration then risks a hidden mucocele.

steps.do: Protect the corneas (temporary tarsorrhaphy or shields). Coronal incision behind the hairline to the preauricular creases, cut parallel to the hair follicles; raise the flap subgaleally or subperiosteally, keeping the pericranium vascularized (raised with the scalp so it does not dry) for the hinge or reconstruction. Laterally, dissect deep to the temporoparietal fascia, on the superficial layer of the deep temporal fascia.
steps.think: The frontal branch of the facial nerve runs on the deep surface of the temporoparietal fascia — the plane beneath that fascia protects it. Supraorbital and supratrochlear bundles leaving through a notch come up with the flap; through a foramen, drill the lower rim of the canal to free them.

steps.do: Outline the sinus with the navigation-derived template and cut the anterior table with a bevel toward the sinus — or drill a line of small holes 0.5–1 cm apart and join them, which removes less bone and lets the flap lock back; fracture the intersinus septum, then hinge the flap down on its pericranium at the orbital rims (or lift it free and keep it in saline).
steps.think: Do the corners of my cuts stay within the sinus on navigation?

steps.do: Treat the disease; if obliterating, remove all mucosa, burr the inner cortex, plug the recess and fill with fat or other material.
steps.think: Every fragment of mucosa left behind is a future mucocele. Fat is the usual filler; avoid hydroxyapatite cement, which infects and needs revision more often.

steps.do: If the posterior table must go (cranialization): remove it with all mucosa, plug the recess, and lay a pericranial flap on the supraorbital and supratrochlear vessels across the floor, sutured to dura, to separate brain from nose.
steps.think: Is the pericranial flap still well perfused when I lay it in?

steps.do: Replace the flap and fix it with titanium plates or wires (a perforation-cut flap may lock without hardware); close in layers.

endpoints: Disease removed; sinus obliterated completely or drained
Flap anatomically replaced
pitfalls: Template error
Residual mucosa under the obliteration
Contour deformity: bossing from a proud or ill-fitting flap or new bone in the saw gap; late depression from over-drilling, poor fixation or resorption
Infection after obliteration for chronic disease (cellulitis, abscess, fistula)
Superficial dissection near the tragus — the frontal branch of the facial nerve and the superficial temporal vessels

procedures.name: Anterior ethmoidal artery ligation (endoscopic or external)
indications: Refractory epistaxis from AEA territory (anterior-superior septum/lateral wall), usually after SPA ligation fails
Devascularization of anterior skull-base tumors
Control of an AEA bleeding during FESS
procedures.corridor: Endoscopic: ethmoid roof at the posterior frontal recess, after a sphenoethmoidectomy has defined the skull base. External: medial orbit through a Lynch/medial canthal or transcaruncular approach along the frontoethmoidal suture.

preop.check: AEA canal position: in the roof or in a mesentery; supraorbital ethmoid cell
preop.why: Endoscopic ligation is straightforward only when the artery hangs below the roof; otherwise an external route is safer.

preop.check: Keros depth
preop.why: Opening the canal medially approaches the lateral lamella.

preop.check: Why the artery is being tied: epistaxis, tumor devascularization or bleeding during FESS
preop.why: For epistaxis an external route with endoscopic assistance is often the safer choice: reaching an artery that runs in the roof endoscopically exposes the skull base just to avoid a small scar. Endoscopic control suits an artery in a mesentery or an ethmoid that is already open.

steps.do: Endoscopic: complete a sphenoethmoidectomy and find the skull base at the sphenoid roof, then follow it forward, opening each cell between its septations (in and out) rather than cutting across them, until the AEA is seen crossing the roof behind the frontal recess.
steps.think: Is the artery accessible below the roof, or would I have to drill the canal next to the lateral lamella? An artery can lie inside a septation — never cut straight across one.

steps.do: Endoscopic: work on the middle of the canal where it crosses the roof — away from the lateral lamella medially and from the anterior ethmoidal foramen laterally. Confirm its course on navigation, thin the canal bone with a diamond bur across a broad front, free the artery from its bony sleeve (a bone-encased artery will not take a clip, even in a mesentery), then clip and/or bipolar it before dividing.
steps.think: Never cut before it is sealed: a divided stump retracts into the orbit. Opening the lamina around the foramen exposes weak periorbita, fat and the medial rectus to the debrider; a narrow drill track near the orbit is how the artery itself gets cut.

steps.do: External: a curved incision midway between the medial canthus and the nasal dorsum, above the medial canthal tendon, broken by a small notch at the level of the canthus to prevent webbing; elevate subperiosteally past the lacrimal sac region and behind the posterior lacrimal crest along the frontoethmoidal suture.
steps.think: Subperiosteal plane only; retract the orbit gently laterally.

steps.do: External: find the AEA tenting the periorbita about 24 mm behind the anterior lacrimal crest; clip or bipolar it, and stop there unless the PEA must be taken.
steps.think: The PEA is about 12 mm further and the optic canal only about 6 mm behind it — do not chase further posteriorly than needed.

steps.do: External: close the deep layers in exact apposition, then skin. After either route, check visual acuity and eye movements hourly for the first 6 hours; mild periorbital bruising is expected.
steps.think: Pain, proptosis, falling vision or restricted movement is an orbital hematoma until proven otherwise.

endpoints: AEA sealed and divided (or clipped) with bleeding controlled
Orbit soft, vision intact
pitfalls: Monopolar cautery near the orbit
Dividing before sealing
Chasing a canal embedded in the roof endoscopically next to the lateral lamella
Removing the lamina papyracea around the anterior ethmoidal foramen endoscopically
Relying on a clip for an artery still encased in bone
Bipolar heat deep in the external approach: the trochlea and superior oblique above, and the optic nerve a few millimetres behind the PEA

procedures.name: Endoscopic orbital decompression
indications: Thyroid eye disease with compressive optic neuropathy, exposure keratopathy or disfiguring proptosis (usually after the active phase)
Emergency relief of orbital hematoma not controlled by canthotomy/cantholysis

Access: drainage of orbital abscess or hematoma, biopsy of indeterminate medial lesions, benign medial tumors ([[p.orbital-tumor-resection]]) and palliative debulking; the first stage of [[p.optic-nerve-decompression]]
procedures.corridor: Medial orbital wall from the frontal recess to the orbital apex and the medial orbital floor medial to the infraorbital nerve, through a complete sphenoethmoidectomy.

preop.check: Frontal recess anatomy
preop.why: Fat prolapse can obstruct it; clear it first and plan to leave the uppermost anterior lamina.

preop.check: Onodi cell, optic canal and skull base
preop.why: Posterior decompression and optic nerve decompression are near the apex.

preop.check: Baseline vision, motility and exophthalmometry
preop.why: Documents compressive neuropathy and pre-existing strabismus; informs whether to preserve the inferomedial strut.

preop.check: Laterality and anesthesia plan
preop.why: Bilateral decompression is usually done at one sitting, and an only-seeing eye is commonly decompressed under general anesthesia; warn the anesthetist against forceful bag-mask ventilation after extubation, which can blow air into the orbit and soft tissues.

steps.do: Complete uncinectomy, a wide maxillary antrostomy to the orbital floor, full sphenoethmoidectomy and frontal recess clearance. Resecting the MT improves exposure of the medial wall, allows more prolapse and eases postoperative cleaning (practice varies).
steps.think: Is the whole lamina exposed from the frontal recess to the sphenoid face, and is the frontal recess clear? In thyroid eye disease the lamina is often bowed medially by orbital pressure — expect it closer than usual.

steps.do: Fracture and remove the lamina papyracea from anterior to the orbital apex, up to just below the frontoethmoidal suture, keeping the periorbita intact.
steps.think: The ethmoidal arteries mark the skull base; preserve them unless they block the decompression. Posterior limit: the sphenoethmoid angle, where the sphenoid face meets the skull base — unless the optic canal is to be opened.

steps.do: Remove the medial orbital floor medial to the infraorbital nerve — elevate the periorbita off it with a ball probe to make a pocket for the curette, then down-fracture — deciding whether to preserve the inferomedial strut.
steps.think: Is the aim maximal proptosis reduction, or optic nerve relief with minimal new diplopia?

steps.do: Incise the periorbita in parallel strips from posterior to anterior (inferior strips first) with a sickle knife, letting fat prolapse.
steps.think: Blade only through periorbita — never a debrider; inferior incisions first so fat does not hide the next ones.

steps.do: For severe proptosis, add a lateral wall decompression through a lateral canthotomy (usually by the orbital surgeon): a balanced medial-plus-lateral decompression.
steps.think: More reduction with less new diplopia than pushing the medial and floor decompression further.

steps.do: For compressive optic neuropathy, extend to the orbital apex and optic canal ([[p.optic-nerve-decompression]]).
steps.think: Is the apex adequately relieved? Avoid heat and pressure on the canal.

steps.do: Finish without nasal packing, so the prolapsed orbital contents are neither pushed back nor compressed.
steps.think: Hemostasis by bipolar and patience, not by packing against the orbit.

endpoints: Medial wall (and medial floor as planned) removed with periorbita opened
Frontal recess kept clear
Optic nerve relieved when indicated
pitfalls: Removing the upper anterior lamina and blocking the frontal recess
Using a debrider on periorbita
Unplanned strut removal causing diplopia
Monopolar cautery near the opened periorbita — bipolar only

procedures.name: Endoscopic transnasal resection of medial orbital tumors
indications: Benign extraconal or intraconal tumors lying medial or inferior to the optic nerve

Lesions lateral to the nerve only when they lie below the plane of resectability — a line from the opposite naris along the long axis of the optic nerve; below it they can be reached without retracting the nerve
Biopsy of indeterminate medial orbital lesions
procedures.corridor: Transethmoidal through the lamina papyracea (and the orbital apex bone), into the extraconal fat and then around the medial rectus into the medial intraconal space, with a posterior septal window for two-surgeon, binostril work.

preop.check: Relation of the tumor to the optic nerve on 3D CT/MRI reconstruction
preop.why: Shows whether it lies medial/inferior to the nerve or below the plane of resectability, and its size and shape.

preop.check: Formal visual fields; a joint plan with ophthalmology (and neurosurgery if the dura or apex may be breached)
preop.why: Baseline for the most feared complication and for the choice of approach.

preop.check: Is a vascular lesion or an ophthalmic artery aneurysm suspected?
preop.why: Angiography only then, not routinely.

steps.do: Complete a maxillary antrostomy, sphenoethmoidectomy and sphenoidotomy to expose the whole medial orbital wall back to the apex.
steps.think: Where is the optic nerve on this side, and is there an Onodi cell?

steps.do: Remove the lamina with fine elevators; thin the thicker palatine and sphenoid bone at the orbital apex and optic canal with an angled diamond bur under irrigation.
steps.think: Heat and pressure near the canal are the danger, not the thin lamina.

steps.do: Open the periorbita with a reverse hockey-stick incision using a sickle knife, keeping the anterior periorbita intact.
steps.think: Intact anterior periorbita helps healing and limits prolapse.

steps.do: Dissect the extraconal fat, where an extraconal tumor is found and removed. Use bipolar only in the extraconal space; warm-water irrigation and saline-soaked patties give hemostasis and retract fat.
steps.think: The ethmoidal neurovascular bundles cross above the medial rectus here.

steps.do: Through a posterior septal window a second surgeon retracts the medial rectus superomedially with a ball probe, exposing the medial intraconal space.
steps.think: Which zone is the tumor in — A (anteroinferior, easiest), B (anterosuperior, beside the ethmoidal vessels) or C (behind the ophthalmic artery's inferomedial muscular trunk, next to the optic nerve, hardest)?

steps.do: Free the tumor from its medial, superior and inferior attachments before dividing the lateral ones, and deliver it anteriorly in a plane parallel to the optic nerve. Do not manipulate the nerve, and do not cauterize or resect intraconal fat.
steps.think: Am I pulling on anything that is tethered to the nerve?

steps.do: After extensive dissection of a mid or anterior orbital lesion, reconstruct the medial wall (e.g. with a nasoseptal flap) to prevent enophthalmos and diplopia from lost orbital volume; small defects near the [[s.annulus-of-zinn|annulus of Zinn]] and optic canal may be left.
steps.think: How much orbital support has this dissection removed?

steps.do: Postoperative: keep any packing off the orbitotomy; serial eye examinations with a low threshold to re-explore; no high-volume irrigation for 2 weeks; a first debridement at days 5–8 only to open the inferior airway, leaving the orbitotomy alone until weeks 3–4.
steps.think: Bleeding or swelling in a closed orbit compresses the nerve — reassess vision, not just comfort.

endpoints: Tumor removed without optic nerve manipulation
Vision and motility at baseline
Medial wall reconstructed when the dissection was extensive
pitfalls: Monopolar cautery anywhere in the orbit; bipolar in the intraconal space
Cauterizing or resecting intraconal fat
Choosing the endoscopic route for a lesion lateral to the nerve and above the plane of resectability
Packing pressed onto the orbitotomy (raised orbital pressure if bleeding or edema follow)

procedures.name: Endoscopic drainage of orbital subperiosteal abscess
indications: Subperiosteal abscess (Chandler III) with visual compromise, large or enlarging abscess, or failure to improve on IV antibiotics
Abscess not meeting criteria for medical management (e.g. older child or adult, non-medial location, frontal sinus involvement)
procedures.corridor: Anterior and posterior ethmoidectomy to the lamina papyracea over the abscess.

preop.check: Contrast CT: abscess position (medial vs superior/lateral), size, gas, frontal involvement
preop.why: Only medial abscesses are reliably reached endoscopically; superior ones need an external route.

preop.check: Visual acuity, colour vision, pupils, motility
preop.why: Sets urgency and the baseline.

steps.do: Decongest heavily, head up; uncinectomy, antrostomy and ethmoidectomy despite inflamed, bleeding mucosa.
steps.think: Bleeding will limit the view: keep the dissection systematic and lateral-plane-first.

steps.do: Remove the lamina papyracea over the abscess, keeping the periorbita intact; pus drains into the ethmoid.
steps.think: Does the drained volume match the CT? If the abscess extends superiorly beyond reach, add an external approach.

steps.do: Culture the pus; open involved frontal or maxillary sinuses; avoid tight packing.
steps.think: Is frontal disease driving a superior collection?

endpoints: Abscess cavity decompressed into the ethmoid
Involved sinuses drained
Vision monitored postoperatively
pitfalls: Incising periorbita and spreading infection into the orbit
Missing a superior or loculated collection

procedures.name: Endoscopic transcribriform approach
indications: Olfactory-groove meningioma (selected)
Esthesioneuroblastoma and sinonasal malignancy involving the cribriform plate
Large anterior skull-base encephaloceles and defects
procedures.corridor: Between the laminae papyraceae from the frontal sinus posterior table to the planum sphenoidale, through a Draf III, bilateral sphenoethmoidectomies and posterior septectomy.

preop.check: MRI/CT extent: dura, brain, orbit (periorbita), frontal sinus
preop.why: Decides whether an endoscopic resection can achieve clear margins.

preop.check: Reconstruction plan: nasoseptal flap availability or pericranial flap
preop.why: Tumor involving the septum rules out the NSF. Pedicled flaps are preferred when radiotherapy will follow; when the septum, posterior ethmoid or pterygopalatine fossa is involved, free fascia and mucosal grafts are taken well away from the tumor.

preop.check: Relation of A2, frontopolar and orbitofrontal arteries to the tumor
preop.why: They lie on the tumor capsule.

steps.do: Infiltrate the pterygopalatine fossa through the greater palatine foramen to reduce bleeding; harvest or preserve reconstruction flaps; bilateral maxillary antrostomies, sphenoethmoidectomies, Draf III and posterior septectomy.
steps.think: Is the whole field from frontal sinus to planum and lamina to lamina exposed?

steps.do: Coagulate and divide the AEA and PEA at the lamina on both sides.
steps.think: Seal before dividing; the stumps must not retract into the orbit.

steps.do: Drill and remove the skull base: fovea, lateral lamellae and cribriform plate, fracturing the crista galli free.
steps.think: Limits: frontal posterior table anteriorly, planum posteriorly, laminae laterally. A tumor confined to one side without septal involvement can be resected unilaterally, preserving smell on the other side.

steps.do: Open the dura around the tumor, divide the falx, debulk centrally and dissect the capsule extracapsularly.
steps.think: Keep arachnoid and vessels on the brain side; which olfactory bulb can be preserved?

steps.do: Reconstruct in layers: dural inlay graft, onlay graft and a vascularized flap covering the whole defect.
steps.think: Does the flap cover every edge of bare bone around the defect? ([[p.skull-base-reconstruction]])

steps.do: Postoperative: a rolled thin Silastic stent in each frontal sinus for 14–21 days; nasal trumpets sutured at the septocolumellar junction for 48–72 hours to divert airflow from the repair; expect crusting for about 3 months (mean about 101 days in one series, longer after larger approaches).
steps.think: Anything that raises nasal pressure — mask ventilation, nose-blowing — can push air through the repair.

endpoints: Tumor resected with dural and bony margins
Watertight multilayer reconstruction
pitfalls: Undersized bone removal that tethers the resection
Coagulating A2 branches on the capsule
Flap too short to cover the frontal end of the defect

procedures.name: Endoscopic repair of anterior skull-base CSF leak
indications: Iatrogenic leak recognized during surgery
Persistent traumatic leak
Spontaneous leak (often with raised intracranial pressure)
Leak after tumor surgery
procedures.corridor: Directly to the defect: cribriform/lateral lamella via the olfactory cleft or ethmoid; ethmoid roof via ethmoidectomy; frontal recess or posterior table via frontal sinusotomy.

preop.check: Confirm CSF (beta-2 transferrin or beta-trace protein)
preop.why: Avoids operating on rhinitis.

preop.check: Thin-section CT — coronal shows cribriform and fovea defects best — (with MRI or cisternography when needed) to localize the defect and any second defect
preop.why: Missed second defects cause failure.

preop.check: Signs of raised intracranial pressure (obesity, empty sella, papilledema)
preop.why: Untreated intracranial hypertension undermines the repair.

preop.check: Anesthesia plan for emergence
